The Grand Master then delivered his Annual Address to the Grand
Lodge, as follows rBRETHBEN OP' THE GBAND LODOlll OP' 0ALll'OBNU. :Another year hae been added to the history of the ages, and once more the representatives of our honored Oraft within this broad jurisdiction have assembled for
oonsnltatlon In reference to the welfare of our cherished Order and to encourage
and cheer each other In the aood work we have to do; and it is with grateful and
devout hearts that we return thanks to the Great Giver of all good for the many
blessings of which, as a 1oolety and as Individuals, we have been the recipients since
laet we met within these aaored walls, dedicated to virtue and universal benevolence.
It la with unfeigned pleasure that I OOQJ!'atulate yon, my brethren, upon the
general proaperlty which prevails throughout out beloved country. The Golden
State, our adopted home, dearer to us, If possible, than the places of our birth, has
been most prosperous during the past year. Mother Earth, ever indulgent, has
yielded her accustomed bounty from the harvest field and the mine, and the skill of
the artisan, co-operating with the enterprise of the merchant, has produced results
which rival the history of the oldest nations of' the world. For e. day or two only in
the past year was the shadow of adversity cast over two or three of our sister
towns, when the elements seemed to combine against them; but the floods soon
stayed, the fires died out, and sturdy enterprise has made them more beautiful than
before. Even the passing financial panic, which swept over us in this city, was but
temporary in its elfect, and the lesson it taught, which could only be learned by
experience, has been of far more benefit to us as 11 people than the injury it caused.
The future to us as e. State is laden with the brightest promises of hope. Every
day new discoveries of hidden wealth are revealed, and, the story of our agricultural
and mineral wee.Ith having now become well known, thousands of people are annually coming to this. most favored land, where the soil Is so fertile and the climate
so varied that the denizens of every zone may here find e. congenial home. Most
cordially do we welcome them among us, and long may they continue to come, for
there is room enough for all who will honestly work. But in the midst of all this
prosperity let us remember that, much having been given us, so much will be
required of us. May we so use that which has been entrusted to our charge that
those who surround us may feel Its beneficent influences. Then will we realize that
living truth that it is" more blessed to give than to receive," for true happiness consists In fixing the. mind upon some object other than our own personal pleasures.
Let us endeavor to do good to others by both kind word and deed ; and let our light
of human sympathy shine far out on the highway of life to encourage and assist the
toiling stranger who is our brother.
The creed of a true Mason is to love all mankind and, as far e.s in his power lies,
to do good unto all, not alone by the mere giving of alms to those who are needy,
but to do good In every possible manner. If a brother is in the wrong, speak not Of
his faults first to another, for no Me.son has the right to speak ill of a brother when
he Is not preaent, however true that which he may say. He should go to him and,
with words of love and klndneBB, remind him of his error, whisper to him good
counsel, and show to him that "Great Light" whence he may glean wisdom to
direct and strength to asslat him In resisting the many temptations by which he is
constantly Atirronnded, and thus win him baok to ·the path of duty and honor.
The prosperity ol our Order throughout the world during the past year has been
most gratifying. The divine principles of fraternity and ben.evolence which it inculcates are bringing to Its support men of every nation and creed. Thoroughly cosmopolitan and universal as It is In Its character, It tends to unite those who would otherwise remain ate. perpetual distance. The Prince of Wales is now Grand Master of
Masons In England, and the humblest member of the Order in the realm meets his

During the past year five applications have been made for dispensations author·
!zing the establishment of new Lodges, of which four were granted, as will be seen
by the report of the Grand Secretary. The fifth application was by a considerably
more than the constitutional number of brethren, from the town of Santa Barbara,
the new Lodge to be called Magnolia Lodge. All were properly recommended by
Santa Barbara Lodge, No.192, but having received the petition but a very short timii
@Ince, I thought It best to refer it to you for your conAideration. In view of the fact
that. one Lodge has beett in existence in that city for several years, with a not any
too large membership, it would seem that, unless some very strong reason was given
for the creation of a new Lodge, the welfare of the Craft would be better promoted
by the affiliation of the applicants with the existing Lodge.
I have granted but six applications for special dispensations during the year, one
of which was to elect a ]\foster, and five of which were to re-ballot for rej_ectcd can1idates. The reiisons 'assigned in the last named cases I deemed sufficient; but I am
fully convinced that only in a case where a serious error bas been committed and
great injustic'e would otherwise result, should such a dispensation be asked ~or or
granted.

appealed to for my opinion I could but recite the law as laid down. But I Paid
that I thought a liberal construction of the law should consider their application
for the recommendation, by anot her Lodge, of their petition for a dispensation the
111me as an application for membership, and should place the brethren named in the

believe that the true spirit of the law intended to encourage non-affiliates to come
Into the fold of Masonry and be active workers, and to protect the Craft from those
who have been drones in the hive, with no ambition to do better.
I have been asked , can a Lodge, In Its character aa a Lodge, incorporate f Also,
would it be proper for a Lodge to subscribe for and hold stock i n a MaKonlc Hall
a11ociation ! and if so, to whom should the stock be Issued f And, further , would a
Lodge be justified in Incurring a debt to subscribe for stock In such an association!
To the first question I answered that I was unable to find any law to prevent a
Lodge from inoorporatiog, but that, In my opinion , such a course wonid be unwise and
Inexpedient and without a precedent in this jurisdiction. To the second and fourth I
replied that there was no Impropriety In a Lodge subscribing for stock In a Masonic
Ha.II association, provided that the Lodge had surplus funds and a majot·!ty of' the
members thought the Investment a j udicious one ; but that to incur a debt for the
purpose of speculating was certainly nnmasonic and by ,any cautious man would be
considered very questionable business policy, and that I deemed it the duty of' the
Master of a Lodge to see that no warrant was drawn upon the treasury if there were
not funds to meet its payment, unless In extreme ca.ses of Masonic n ecessity or
charity. To the third I responded that Lodges, under their present orgamzation
here, could only hold stock as property through trustees who had been elected or
appointed for that purpose by the Lodge. Iu this connection I may add that there
Is a great diversity of opinion In dllferent Lodges as to the relation which the tr ustees
bear to the Lodge, and as to the proper mode of eelectlog them. Should the by-laws
provide for their election or appointment, or should it be by resolution of the Lodge,
duly recorded? Aud have they, the trustees, power to buy and sell property for or
of the Lodge without the sanction of that body? I answered that I thought it quite '
proper that the trustees should be elected by the Lodge, and that a r esolution
making that provision would answer every purpose. While I gave my opinion• as to
the acts of the trustees, I do not think them worth repeating, as they would not,
perhaps, be considered very good authority by the Committee on Jurleprudenoe or
a court of equity. I would, however, recommend that the Grand Lodge adopt some
general regulation upon the aubject of selecting trustees by the subordinate Lodges
and defining their duties.
I have approved quite a large numb~r of amendments to the by-lawa of Lodgea,
and in a few cases have declined to approve those submitted to me for reasons which
I deemed sufficient. In two Instances have I given m,y approval contrary to my own
judgment. I should have withheld It until I bad submitted them to you for
your action, had not the preqedent been established by the approval of similar amendments from other Lodges In former years, One case was the Increasing or the fee for
degrees to one hundred do!lara and of the affiliation fee to tweoty·flve dollars. The
other case Increased the affiliation fee to twenty dollara. These amendments are in
striking contrast with the great majority of amendments adopted by other Lodges,
which have reduced the fee fbr degrees to the minimum rate fixed by the Con•titution, and have entirely abolished the affiliation fee or fixed it at the nominal sum of
one dollar. This is, I think, more in harmony with the true spirit of our Order. It ie
not money that commends a man to become a Mason, and nothing bearing a resem··
blance to a golden barrier should be placed to guard the entn .nce ; for when one
knocks at the door of Masonry the first t ime for admission, in search of that light

1111 M. '. W. •• Grand Lodge of Oal.ifornia : I iilll pleased to report that, from personal observation and from snch reports of

urd11noe with our regulation and that a great majority are doing well. During
I ,yoar Just closed I have instructed an unusual number of brethren in the work and
h 1 lurt1. Masters elect have come from remote parts of the State to qualify them·
lu1, In some instances Lodges have appropriated a sufficient amount to defray
Iha Ir expenses to and from, and during their stay in, San Francisco, while obtainiog
Iha work. I have always cheerfully instructed all who II.ave come to me; but am
l1111l111od to think that if the amount expended in this manner had been used in
1
Ina an Inspector to visit the Lodge, where he could have instructed all its officers,
Iha Lodge would have derived much greater benefit; because many, instead of one,
uuld have become familiar with the ritual. Io all cases I have endeavored to
l11111re1K upon the minds of those Masters who appeared for Instruction the necessity,
Ill &1hlltlon to instructing their subordinate officers In their several duties, of Imparting
lh• tlltlre work to some competent brother, so that, in case of the Master's removal
m &bMence, some one present would be qualified to give Instruction, and the Lodge
ould not have wasted its money. The following is an abstract of the information
hloh bas been received from the officers in charge of districts: Jn1pector JOHN A. WATSON, of the first district, reports having visited all the
I d;ts therein except Orescent Lodge, No. 45, which, on account of distance and
111 roughness of the trail, he was unable to attend. The Lodges, he says, are all in
toll condition and !'air working order, and he had not been called upon to perform
111y 11npleasant official duty.
Jn1pector ROBERT H. F, VA.RIEL visited officially but three of the seven Lodges com11rl~lng the fourth district. He reports those as in excellent condition in all respects,
11111 regrets that, on account of the demands of business, he was prevented from
¥hiltlng the other four, He recommends that that district, comprising the counties
r Plumas and Lassen, be divided- Plumas forming one, and LBBaen, with SurpriJle
Valley Lodge, No. 225, another-inasmuch as the two counties are separated by a
f1n11e of lofty mountains which, in the winter season, form an almost insuperable
llarrler to communication. The roads connecting said counties are untraveled by
••ll·ooaches or other public conveyances, so that when a Master of Lassen desires
outlficate of qualification from an Inspector in Plumas, he must be at considerable
lull and expense to obtain it. The reasons given for the proposed division appear to
ll11ood.
Jn1pector ORRIN W. HoLLEl!IBEOK, of the seventh district, reporta that most of
lb• Masters therein were dnly examined by him before their installation. The
otptlons were those who had been re·eleoted and whom he allowed to be
lt111t111led without a re-examination, as he supposed at the time that, by a certain

Ihm being called to his notice, as soon as p acticable thereafter all who ha.d been
111mpted were subjected to examination. He visited each Lodge in the district,
11cept .Dibble, No. 109, the Master of whioh expressed a doubt as to his ability to
1•t enough members together to exemplify the work. The once l!ourishing town of
"'11111a 1 where the Lodge is located, has now but a small population of white men,
Iba mines being operated by Chinamen; and the membership of the Lodge is scattered and fast falling off. Th" brethren are seriously considering the propriety of
1urrenderiog their charter. Under the circumstances, he did not visit them, as he
oonld be of no service. Bro. HOLLENBECK reports In detail the standing of each
1,od11e In the work. Less than half the Lodges in his district rank as first-class;
ruur of them work poorly; the remainder do f11ir work. He does not doubt, how.
ner, that the Lodges of the seventh district will compare favorably with the same

Inspector BOLON W, CB.uaus, ot the twenty-1lxth, has two Lodges in hie district,
one at Ban Diego, the other at Pre1oott, In Arizona Territory. Of San Diego Lodge
he report., "that the Master and all the oftloera are thoroughly posted in the

year that It wu poulble for him to have gone there.
In mv seneral ln1trnotlon1 to Lodges, I have recommended .the practice of pre·
aentlog to each Initiate a lamb·skln, or white teather apron, with the name
of the owner and the dates ot hie initiation, passing, and raising, inscribed
thereon beneath the flap. I wonld earnestly urge this practice by all the Lodges of
the j11rl1dlotlon. Thia emblem of innocence and badge of a Mason, when given to
the candidate, 11 put away among his most cherished treasures, and is never seen
., wlthont oan1logthe mo•t pleasurable emotions to thrill his bosom. Bro. MA.OKEY says:
There 11 no one of the symbols of speculative Masonry more lmportant ·in Its
teaching•, or more Interesting in its history, than the lamb-•kin or white leather apron.
Commencing Its lessons at an early period in the M&.son's progress, it is impressed
upon his memory as the first gift which he receives, the first symbol which is explained
to him, and the first tangible evidence which he possesses of his admission into the
Fraternity. Whatever may be his futnre advancement In the roral art, Into whatsoever
deeper arcana his devotion to the myetic institution or his thirst for knowledge may
subsequently lead him, with the lamb-skin apron he will never part.
/To show how much good has been accomplished by the practice of presenting
the lamb-skin to initiates, I will relate the following incidents, which have come
under my own observation. A. certain man, before leaving his old home in the East,
had been made a Mason, bot since coming to the Pacific Coast had not visited a
Lodge, and had fallen into evil paths and been led into dissipation. One day, when
looking over some articles in his trunk, be came upon a forgotten package which,
when opened, was found to contain bis lamb-skin apron-for the Lodge wherein he
was made a Mason had made It a custom to present each member with this emblem
of Masonry. The sight of the spotless vestment; more ancient than the golden fleece
' or Roman eagle, aroused a fiood of recollection in his bosom. In imagination be was
carried back to bis old home, where he had been honored and respected,-to the
time when he stood in the north-east corner, a just and upright man, where it had been
given him strictly in charge ever to act and walk as such. He asked himself whether
he had fulfilled the charge 1-whether be had walked as an upright man? He felt that
he had not. The spark of manhood which still lingered in his bosom waa strong
enough to kindle a glowing fire. He put the apron away and went forth, determined
to oonqner the terrible demon that bad been leading him on to the abyss of destruc·
tlon. He made himself known to some of the Masons of this city, frankly admitted
his wrong doing, and asked them to assist him in reforming. A helping hand was
extended, t11f 1troog grip was given him, and by its aid he was lifted out of the
depth& Into which he had fallen, and once more stood a just and upright man. He
is now honored and respected by the workmen in the Temple, instead of being an
outcaet and dl•iraoed. The other case occurred in the interior of Mexico. A.
brother wae travellni through that country, where he contracted a fever and soon
became dellrloua. Thoae with whom he was domiciled examined his baggage for
the purpoee ot getting him 1111mo olean linen, and tound a lamb·skin apron. It was
, immedlatel7 reooinlmed, for thoH Into whose handa he had fallen were Masons. It
is needless to 11y how tenderl7 he w111 oared for ; bow oarefully his nurses attended
upon him until the last moment oame; and then, how reverently they closed his eyes
and laid hlm beneath the earth. The written reoord on the lamb-skin furnished the
brethren with the neoeeaary lntormatlon to communicate wit~te Lodge of the
deceased, and send to hie friends 1uoh property 118 he left behind.

ARKANSAS.

The Grand Lodge of this State commenced its thirty,sixth Annnal Communication
In the city of Little Rook, on the nineteenth day of October, 1874.,-the M.-. W.·.
G. A. DANNELLY, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.'. w. .. LUKE E. BARBER being
Grand Secretary. Representatives were present from one hundred and six Lodges.
The Grand Master, in bis Address, announced that be had issued eighteen dispen~
eations for the formation of new Lodge.a during the :11ear. He bad been called upon
to decide many questions of Masonic law and usage, and presented his decisions for
the consideration of the Grand Lodge, which approved most of them. They
announce no new doctrine, but seem to us in keeping with the landmarks and tradi·
tions of the Order.
St. J obn's College, established under the auspices of the Grand Lodge for the
education of the orphan sons of Masons, is not in as prosperous condition as could
be wished, although its prospects are brightening to some extent. The Committee
on Education, in their report of its condition, sayWe find the financial condition of the College unflattering-a debt of $4878.16
created for improvements and repairs two years ago, still unpaid, and no money on
hand for the payment of the professors. The incidental expenses have been fOTtunately met by our skillful lioancial agent, through advance payments made upon lots
sold. With a property worth $119,9W.87, reinforced with the surplus revenue arising
from nearly 350 Lodges, it is not probable that any very extreme measures will have
to be adopted to avert bankruptcy. The reduction in the number of professors and
of the salaries of those retained, coupled with other ·retrenchments, has reduced the
expenses over three thonsand dollars. This exhibit of the inauguration of a system
of economy is gratifying, and if steadily pursued must leall. to substantial results.
The endowment fund, amounting to $43,000, is still intact, and no such extreme exigen~ exists as to inspire a. fear .that it will have to be disturbed.

In the year 1873-4 there were one hundred and seven students In attende.noe &t
the college, six of whom were gradnated. The Committee on Masonic Law and
U.age define the status of a brother Bnspended for the non-payment of dun as
follows:!. Mason suspended for non-payment of dues, merely, is placed in the attitude of
1 wllll'ully non-affiliated Mason. He has no claims upon any Lodge, nor has he auy
Lodge privileges. He cannot sit in the Lodge that suspends him, or any other Lodge,
without permission of the Lodge, until he is restored to membership. He is merely
an Individual Mason at large, and other :Masons are not debarred from holding
Ma1onic intercourse with him.
Thie may be sound doctrine In Arkansas, but we hardly think it w{ll pass as such
In &ny other part of the Masonic world. A Mason under suspension of any kind is
not In "good standing." How then can any LDdge admit him to sit among the
brethren?. He is suspended from all the rights and privileges of Masonry. The only
difference between suspension for non-payment of dues and suspension for unmasonlc
conduct is, that It is always in the power of the brother so suspended to restore
himself to good standing by paying bis indebtedness, while the one suspended for
the other cause must call upon the Lodge, or Grand Lodge, for restoration.
In regard to the use of Masonic Halls for e.ny other than Masonic purposes, the
111me committee say-" It is desecration." '.!'here is no Report on Correspondence,

On the subject of Religion and Masonry, Bro. WEBBER discourses lo the following
n11111ner :•
In looking over the proceedings of sister Grand Jurisdictions, I observe discus·
11lnn" which, it seems to me, are entirely foreign to our Institution. Some seek to
11rove that Masonry 1~. and others that it is not, religion. Which le right depends upon
lhe definition which is given to the term. The dispute is rather a dispute about
hrms than a dispute about principles. There are many different religions In the
World,. and each adjudges all the rest wrong, Why should we dispute about such
que1t1ons? Masonry has been well defined to be "a universal system whi<'h teaches
lbe relative and social duties of man on a broad, extensive basis of general philan·
hropy." Within that definition every lover of hla kind, every one who is willing to
nve his neighbor as himself, or to do anto otherr as he would have others do unto
him, can see that Masonry is right. no matter wbeth~r, as a technical reliirlonist, he
lrn a Jew, a Mahommedan, a Christian, a follower of Zoroaster, Confucius, or
The inhabitants of all climes and the men or every worship may join with
'Brahma.
Ma~ons without heRring thRt which will conflict with I.heir pecnltar Ideas. As men,
•• citizens, as members of ecclesiastical organizations, clift'crences may exist
b1tween us. With those differences we, as Masons, have nothing to do , and a di•·
01111ion of those difference& should find no place In our Lodge-rooms. When we
meet 11s Masons, we meet as children of one common Father, u brothers laboring
fDr one common end. If we ere asked for our creed, we reply," Faith, Hope, and
Clllarity." If we are asked for the tenets of our profession. we answer, "Brotherly
I.eve, Relief, ancl Truth.'' If' we are asked what principles guide u1 lo our inter·
course with humanity and in our progress through life, we an~wer," Temperance,
Fortitude, Prudence, and Justice." IC there be any who say that oqr creed la
founded in error, th11t our tenets are not entitled to their r~spect, and that the prln·
olples guiding us through life are not well adapted to benefit humanity, we point
tfiem to the history of onr ln•t'tutions which ante·dates human records, and Hk:
Who is he that dare put his individual opinion against the experience of the pBRt 1
Mo believing, let our practice be m11de to conform to our professions: we serve God
ho•t when we best serve our fellow men. "Be not weary .in well doing, for In due
eeason ye shall reap, If ye faint not."

The Grand Lodge of Minnesota began its twenty-second Annual Communication in
the city of St. Paul, on the twelfth day of January, 1875,-the M.·. W.·. CHARLl!B
GRISWOLD, Grand Ma1ter, presiding, and the R.·. w... EDWIN D. B. PORTER being

The Grand Maater's Address is an able and interesting paper, abounding in sound
Ideas, well expressed. He announces the death of Bro. ALFRED E. AKES, the first
Grand Master of the Grand Lodge or Minnesota. The proceedings are embellished
with his Dortrait, and contain a mourning page in honQr of his memory. During
the year he had div.!ded the State Into eleven Masonic Districts, and had appointed
a District Deputy Grand Master for each. Dispensations had been issued for the
formation of ten new Lodges.
Several decisions Bre reported. From these we learn that the law in Minnesota
punishes non-payment of. dues by striking the name of the delfoquent from the roll,
which simply "makes him a non·afllliate, but does not suspend him." He can, on
paying up the dellnqoent dues, present his petition for afllliation. Here we suspend
a brother for non-payment of dues, but he is restored to good standing by the simple
process of squaring up his account.
In 1853 the Grand Lodge became an Incorporate body, under the provlslona of
an Act of the Territorial Legislature. The Grand Master has concluded that It was
a mistake, and might result in great Inconvenience and annoyance. He saysThat it Is not well for either Grand or subordinate Lodges to become bodies cor·
porate. and that the best course for ns to por•ne is, if possible, to obtain legislation
repealing the act under which we became such. · A corporate body is a creature or
the civil law, and any and all o! its affairs may be dragged into the courts in a variety
of ways and upon various pretei<ts. For instance, a brother member of our Grand
Lodge, or of one of its subordinates. is iiuilty ofsome gross misdemeanor; charges are
preferred-he is tried, and expelled; under the plea that the sentence was unduly
severe and·the act of the Lodge damaging to his reputation, he applies to the courts
for relief; they may, if they see fit, order the reinstatement of the aggrieved brother,
and the Lodge which pronounced tlte aforesaid sentence find hanging over its head a
judgment for damages to the amount of some hundreds or thousands of dollars.
Our by-laws, too, may· be subjected to revision by the same powers, or a con·
tested election case may arise, and the civil courts be at last left to determine who
shall fill the " Oriental Ohair." The above. cases are not quite all hypothetical, but
have in certain organizations of a secret character had their counterpart.
Aiiatn, old Masons will remember well scenes of a similar nature enacted during
the Morgan excitement, when the strong arm of the civil law was stretched forth
and officers and members of Grand and subordinate Lodges, incorporated under
State laws, were summoned to appear and produce records and Dapers, nod ques·
tioned with reference to everything pertaining to the business ·and work or the
Lodge, Ill. any body corporate similar scenes are liable to transpire. For these and
other reasons which might be given, I have been forced to the conclusion that the
custom of Incorporating Masonic Lodges Is one that should fall into Slleedy dliuse.
Notwithstanding oar belief that the work of conferring the degrees is pretty
thoroughly done in C&lifornia, nnder our present system of District Inspectnrs-no
brother being permitted to advance until he has shown reasonable proficiency in the
preceding degree-yet it may not be amiss to reproduce a portion of Bro. GRISWOLD'S
remarks on the subject of" Hnrrylng tile Work." He saysThere is an evil in our midst which, in our humble opinion, is somewhat seriouB In
its nature, and to the consideration of which we invite your careful attention, vii.:
the practice so common among us of hurrying candidates through the degrees.
Troe. we have a law which·was intended to remedy the evil of which we speak, and
which forbids the conferring of more than one degree upon a candidate at the same

The Grand Master's Address ls a lengthy and able production, occupying eighteen
l'AllOM of the proceedings. He alludes to the completion of the magnificent Temple
ha New York, and, having congratulated the Oraft thereon, says ·
More than usual importance attaches t o our ceremonies at this tim e, because of
Uan Interest t hat has been displayed recently in various par ts of the Old World in our

With t hese instanees of increasing interest in our F ra ternity, it seems particularly opportune Ll1at our Temple should be completed Just at this time, that we, In
the great metropolis of the Western World, sliould be able to send back to our
brethren of the East the evidence that the affections, and hopes, and interests of
Masons in this land are as bright as those of older civilizations •
The Temple was dedicated on tbe second day of the Communication, with great
pomp a nd in the presence of an immense concourse of brethren. .An address was
dtllvered on the occasion by Past Grand Master JOHN L. LEWIB, It was a brilliant
production, and had we space we should re-p roduce it entfre. We quote the closing
paragraphs :It may be thought-it Is thought-that the ceremonies and the events of this hour
atroct only the brethren of the mystic tie. If it were no more than this, we could
1tlll rejoice with a joy unspeakable . But these are so deeply entwined with our
oommon humanity, so intimately connected with a higher civilization , so pregnant
with considerations that affect not only our Craft, buc the ma~s of our na1ionality,
\bat it wel'e false t o duty to refrain from their presentation.
With questions of State, or the administrations of governments, and with religious
1to1B, or t heir p eculiar creeds, our institution, In its sphere of du ty, has no part or
lot. Tolerance t-0 a ll and bias towards none, are its cardinal principles of belief and
aotlon-iea ving every brother free to act according to the dictates of hie own cou1olence, only requifing him to be loyal to his country, true to his fellow·men, and
obedient t o his God. But we are deeply concerned in that which s treets character
Ind stability of govemments, and the peace and purtt.y .of churches in their effects
u11on the happlneas of mankind. The ad vocates of peace, we have a vowed before
h gh Beaven that the sword shall not devour fore ver; t hat toleration shall be the
rractice, as it is the rule, in this free land ; and that art and science 43hall receive
hat protection and encouragement which they so eminently require in t heir ~trugglea
with a worldly spirit. But these , and a myriad of other mora l euds, are by us
advanced on.ly by moral means and the power of associated effort directed through
ihat proper and legitimate channel. For other ends and other objects, connected
with the tenderest offices of hum11nity a nd the better feelings of our nature, we
point not boastingly, bot truthfully, t o our p ast history. When did the storm cind the
'em pest devastatu- when did confiagration rage fiercely and wildly - when did
famine a nd pestilence send forth their sad wails npon the lllden breeze-that they did
not meet wi th a resp onse as r~Bdy as the need was lmmiuent, a nd as g reat as was
thu extent of the want, from the large, warm heart of Masonry which paused not
tu Inquire into questions of clime or social condition, of r eligious or political belief?
Bald we not tr uly, then, that the great body of our !'e llow-citizens have a deep and
abiding interest with us? Said we not truly, that this temple just now so solemnly
dedicated, was to be the shrine of some of the noblest virtnes of our common
h11manity ?
.
The pageant of this hour will soon be over and be amongst the things of the past;
but our mission will never pass away. It may be that some earnest spirits are looking for the advent of that glorious day when there shall come sounding upon the

ear, and impressing the inmost soul, voices soft and sweet as those of the winged
messengers of the skies, yet clear and distinct as the trump of the arch-angel, proclaiming-" Peace on earth, and good will to men I'" Then, Indeed, would one portion of our miRsiou be fultllled, and we should be left free to pursue the bumble, but
ever·rerurring duty of wiping away the mourner's tear, of shielding and protecting
helpless orphanBge, and of causing the lone heart and the lonelier hearth once more
to Ile lit up with gladness, and the smile of joy to · come in the morning, after the
long night of wearlnesR and wDe. But we are constrained to believe that we -shall
not behold those halcyon days, and that we must continue to mini•ter in our lowly,
but happy sphere, till the mists of time melt away at the sunlight and dawn of
eternity.
And if, In 10 doing, we pursae our own customs, are governed by our own simple
regulations, shrnud our movements in a veil of secresy, only to be torn away upon
th~ morning of the resurrection, when everything secret shall be made manifest,
deem u1 not fantastic or frivolous, but simply desirous to presel've those safeguards
which, in this evil world are honestly reqmred as a protection against craft and guile,
and to strengthen those ties which bind us together as fellow-laborers in the cause of
justice and humanity. If these peculiarities were laid aside, it would destroy our
peace and harmony, expose us to be the prey of the designiIJg and unprincipled, and
pervert the objects and designs of our institution into those of unholy ambition or
selfish desire of/ublic applause. Then the good we would do would be aimless and
purposeless, an the good we oould do be a~ vain and idle as the da~hing of the
waves upon the sands or the rock·bound shores.
Long then may this Temple stand, not only as the home shelter of the Craftsman,
but the temple indeed of the Virtues ; enshrining not like those of ol<l, the sculp·
tured images of false goods, but being the council-chamber and central laboratory ?f
the gootl and true, devising benefits for their fellow-men; honored as it has been m
its dedication, by the presence and sympathy of the wise and the gifted, the learned
Bild distiIJguishod of sister jurisdictions, so gladly and heartily welcomed here to-day,
and crowning us with two-fold honor. Long, we repeat, may this Temple stand, a
beacon-light, not, indeed, upon the shore, darting its rays npon the wilderness of
waters, but a beacon-light in the heart of this great metropolis; shedding its refulgent
splendor upon the broader ocean of eternity, and an earthly memorial .of that
. "spiritual building-that house not made with hands-eternal in the heavens:'

The Grand Master reports alxty·slx decisions on questions of law and usage.
We give the gist of a few of those having general application:Tbe Master of a Lodge should be Installed after each re-election.
The physical qualifications of a candidate- for Masonry cannot be determined
by the Grand Master.
The Grand Master cannot Issue a di~peneatlon allowing a Lodge to disobey a
landmark of :Masonry.
Whether a candidate is such" a hale man, sound, not deformed or dismembered,"
as the landmarks of Masonry prescribe to be eli~ible material for the temple, is a
question that must be settled by the conscientious judgment of the Master and
each brother of the Lodge. If the Master of a Lodge is not satisfied, after thor·
oughly and scrupulously considering the matter, that the candidate Is such a man,
it will be his duty to reject him.

In Ohio delinquents are ezpelled for non-payment of dues. The Grand Master
thinks the penalty too severe for the offense, and suggests that it be changed to suspe111lon. We beg to recommend to our Ohio brethren the California law in this matter. The penalty here is suspension, but the suspended brother can restore himself
to iiood standing by simply paying what he owes. The law works admirabJy, for if
a brother is really unable to pay his dues, they ere remitted, as they ought to b"e,
The receipts for the year amounted to $12 ,040 60, and the expenditures were

Lodge, we think, erred in adopting the report. A worthy distressed brother is entitled to relief at the hands of his Lodge, and If it be affQTded by others, the Lodge
ought to foot the bill. We think this action is fuli' of uncharitableness.

The Grand .:Master's Address is well worthy of his reputation for a high order of
ability, and shows·that he has earrvietly devoted himself to the active discharge of
tbe responsible duties of his position. Tb11 Craft are represented to be harmonious
and prosperous, and generally doing good square work. He had received five appli·
cations for dispensations to establish new · Lodges, two of which be had granteddecUning to grant the others on' what seems to us just grounds. The majority of
the petitioners for one were members of a Lodge that was laboring under financial
embarrassments, and he deemed it" unwise to permit them t~ withdraw until their
tlnancial matters were fully adjusted." Six out of the seven petitioners for another,
resided from nineteen to thirty miles from the proposed location. Thia, tog~ther
with the fact that the neighborhood was sparsely settled, was Just cause of appre•
h4lnsiou as to its success If established. He had visitited twenty-one Lodges during
the year.
Only four decisions on questions of law are reported, all which were approved
by the Grand Lodge, as follows:1. A brother who signs a petition to the Grand Master for a dispensation to
establish a new Lodge, cannot apply for affiliation to any other Lodge during t he
oontinuance of such dispensation. When a charter is granted, it Is optional with
him either to sign the petition for a charter which, If granted, would complete his
rnem bershlp, or to apply for affiliation to any other Lodge he might select.
2. The statua of a brother who has received the Master Mason degree In a Lodge
other than that in which he was entered , eit her by consent or request, Is that of a
non·a!Hliate until he signs the by-laws; and It is competent for any J,odge to entertain his petition for affiliation, accompanied with a statement showing why he Is not
lo possession of a dlmlt.
3. The refusal of a Master :Mason's widow to allow the Fraternity to perrorm the
burial service, and neglecting other kind offices tendered her in her hour of desola·
tlpn and a!Hlction, will not debar her at any subsequent time, so long as she remains
Ills widow, to claim r elief when in distress, for herself or children; nor will any act
or word of here release the Fraternity from their obligations to respond. The right
of relief inures to her by virtue of her husband's good standing at the time of' his
death, and t he olalm should be respected.
4. It is Inconsistent with the spirit and intent of Masonry for a Lodge to entertain
11ny proposition to provide or arrange, by the appointment of committees or other·
wise , for Masonic balls. Festivities of this character are wholly foreign t.o the purpose for which Lodgea are congregated, and are very liable to produce confusion
among the Craft, even if unanimity prevailed; t he act of the Lodge authorizing and
consenting to such festivities, virtually implies that the expenses incurred thereby
will be assumed by the Lodge, which Is forbidden by Standing Regulation, No. S, of
the Grand Lodge.
One of the Lodges voted a present of a lamb-skin apr on to a brother who had
been active In establishing the Lodge. Some member of the Lodge appealed from
this action to .the Grand Master, on the ground that no property belo11gl11g to the
Lodge could be voted away, except for charitable purposes. The Grand Master
sustained the Lodge.
Twenty years ago the Grand Lodge created an educational fund , with the lnten·
\Ion, at some future day, of establishing an institution of learning. Then the sbhool
facilities of the State were limited; now , however, it is well supplied with schools
and colleges, and there is no longer any neceBBity for oarrylng out the enter prlae.
The fund has Increased to $13,000, and the Grand Master recommended that this be
converted into .a oharlty fund. The Grand Lodge declined to adopt the suggestion.

The Committee on Jurisprudence reported on the "Revision of the Edicts of the

more important points:In the absence of the Master and Wardens of a Lodge, the duties of the Chair
shall devolve on the oldest Past Master present. Jn the absence of Master, Wardens
and Past Masters, the members, accordmg to seniority, may fill the Chair, and have
all the rights of a regularly installed Master I !
Lodges possess the power to deal with members for non-payment of dues, and
may dtop from the roll, suspend or expel delinquents, or excuse them.
No Lodge shall bear the name of any living person.
Tlie Master, or one of the Wardens, mast deliver one of the three lectures at least;
once in each month.
The min!Ulum sum for conferring the degrees shall be thirty dollars.
No Lodge shall confer the degrees on more than one candidate at the same time.
No brother can be elected Master of a Lodge unless be shall have regularly served
as Warden.
The habit of drunkenness should not be tolerated among the members of a subordinate Lodge, and suspension for minor offenses, and expulsion for a confirmed
habit of druokenoesB, should be invariably adopted.
.
For a persistent habit of profane swearing, it is recommended that suspeDBlOD or
expulsion be invariably adopted.
Gambling Is deddedly nomasonio and unbecoming, and should not be tolerated
by any subordinate Lodge.

UTAH.
In a neatly printed and well arranged pamphlet of one hundred and sixty-four
pages, we have the proceedings of the Grand Lodge of Utah, at its third Annual
Communication, held in Salt Lake City ou the tenth day of November, 1874,-the
M.·. W.·. LOUIS COHN, Grand Master, presiding, and the R. ·• W.·. CHRIBTOPHSB
DIEHL being Grand Secretary. All the Lodges were represented.
The Grand Master's .A:ddress occupies twelve pages of tbe proceedings, and
abounds with noble sentiments and wholesome advice to the Craft. He urges the
Lodges to inspect well all the material offered and exercise strict discipline over
their members. He complains of the meager attendance at Lodge meetings and
attributes it to the fact that most of the brethren, as soon as they have received the
third degree, hasten to gain admission into the Chapter and .Oommandery, and when
that has been accomplished, neglect the Lodge. Bro. COHN says-•' Standing on his
lofty pinnacle, the young Knight Templar of two or three mouths standing 11onsiders
himself a very high Mason indeed, and lhe Blue Lodge is totally ignored, or looked
upon as something only fit for the lower ranks of the Order."
The Grand Secretary presented an elaborate report of the transactions of his
office, and also a report as Librarian. From the former we learn that there are (so
far as could be ascertained) two hundred and twelve Masons in Utah who are con·
tributing members of Lodges in other jurisdictions, and ninety-five non-affiliates. The
library contains one hundred and seventy-nine volumes.

The Grand Lodge of Vermont held its Aouoal Communication in the city of Burlington, 9n the tenth day of June, 1874,-the M.·. W.·. PARK DAvra, Grand Master,

The Grand Master's Address is au able and earnest paper and shows him to be
imbued with the true spirit of Masonry. It is devoted to the local affairs of his jnris·
diction, and hence we find bot little In it to reproduce. We cannot refrain, however,
from quoting the following:·
Belief in God is the life-giving principle in Masonry. It is the grand object of
Masonic teachings. lt inspires our ceremonies, which otherwise would be but duil
routine with a symbolism of God's universal love and mercy for His creatures. · It
is this that makes Masonry universal- adapting It to the needs of all men. Wherever
au altar is erected to the known and true God, there cau our altar stand, with its
infiuences purifying the lives of our members with lessons of obedience and love to
the Supreme Being. Its inflneuces are silent, gradual, yet effective, comtantly training the man, developing his heart, aod teaching him to live a life of morality and
virtue. When the mind is raised upward~ towards God, with implicit faith in Him,
he is taught to regard h•• fellow-man as his brother ; and when taught to submit to
Godrs government he is led to a just regard of the rights of his brethren. From
this source flows all . the benefits of our mstitutiou-subduing the soul in.to awe for
God as our Father, RUd filling the heart with kind regard for man as our brother. In
all things, then, should His Almighty hand ever be recognized, and His sacred name
never profaned by Masons.
The Grand Master announces the death of a veteran Craftsman- Bro. WILLIAM:
BBIOOSB- who was made a Mason in 1820, and stood " firmest when the storm of

a brother present would black-ball the applicant. The Master "called oil"' the
Lodge and the objecting brother left; then the Lodge was "called on" and the
applicant was elected to receive the degrees, and at a special meeting the first
degree was conferred upon him. The offending Master was afterwards restored
to his position by the Grand Master. We think he ought to have been expelled,
for we can imagine no more flagrant o:lfense than that of which he was guilty,

To the M.-. W.·. Grand Lodge of Oalifornia :Three documenla from the Grand Orient of Hungary were referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence, viz.:A circular letter under date of April 2d, 1878, announcing its organization under
pennission of the Austrian Government, giving a list of its officers and members,
and asking recognition and an exchange of Representatives:
A letter dated January 2d, 1875, proposing the name of Bro. the Baron FlllIDEBIO
PoDHANICZXY, a member of the Council of the Order, for appointment OB the Representative of this Grand Lodge near that Grand Orient, and uking that we name some
member of our Graud Lodge for appointment 118 Beprel!entative of that Grand Orient
here:
And a letter dated July 21st. 1875, relating to the same matters mentioned in the
last preceding communication.
The committee have carefully considered these papers and respectfully report
that the Grand Orient of Hungary appears to have been properly organized at Pesth,
in the Kingdom of Hungary, on the twenty-sixth day o! November, 1871, with the
m... Bro. GEOBOB Jo.6.llNOVIOS as Gra.nd :Muter, and the Ill... Bro. LADISLAS

111

HoLLOS as Secretary General, and that it is a regularly established and jnst ~asonio
Body, deserving recognition. All the Lodges which united in the organization of this
Grand Orient had been established by the Grand Orient of France, which, on the
i\Venty-third day of December, 1871, gave formal recognition to the new Grand
Orient.
We are pleased to see that the Grand Orient of Hungary so far recognized
the American doctrine of Grand Locfge jurisdiction and sovereignty as to declare, in
one of the articles of its Constitution, that it would not establish any Lodge in any
foreign country in which a Grand :Muonic Power had been organized, and that it

The Committee oµ Jurisprudence have given careful consideration to the circular
letter from the United Grand Orient of Lusitania regarding its relations with the
Grand Orient of Spain, and respectfully report that they find nothing in the letter
which requires action on the part of this Grand Lodge. They are sorry that anything
should have occurred to interrupt the harmony which form11rly existed in the rela.tions of those two Grand Bodies, but can do nothing toward settling their differences.
From the paper received it appears that, during the reign of Isabella II, late
Queen of Spain, the government opposed the establishment of Masonic Lodges; that
all the Lodges then existing there were working ~der charters granted by foreign
Grand Bodies; and that the United Grand Orient of Lusitania had established Lodges
at Seville, Cadiz, and Madrid. We learn that, after the revolution of 1868, a Grand
Orient of Spain was established which, in 1872, was· formally recognized by the
United Grand Orient of Lusitania; that those two Grand Bodies entered into a compact or treaty by which it was stipulated that their jurisdiction should be concurrent
over Spain and Portugal; and that each should 'retain the Lodges of its own obedience and be allowed to establish new Lodges in both Kingdoms. ·
Subsequently, difficulties, which appear to have been purely of a political charac:
ter, arose which interrupted their harmonions relations. Those difficulties they
must settle in their own way, and wo hope, for the good name of Masonry, that they
may be very presently adjnsted.

To the M. •• W.•• Grand Lodge of Oaliforni a:Under date of January lSth, 1875, the Grand Lodge of Colombia, South America,
addressed a circular letter to the Grand Lodge of California, (aud we presume to all
the Grand Lodges of the United States), expressing its sympathy with and its earnest
desire for the success of the Cubans in their long-continued straggle for independence,
and asking that this Grand Lodge join with it in using its influence, as a :Masonic
power, to induce the Spanish Government to recognize the independence of Cuba.
That circular was referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence and, having ;received
careful consideration, the committee respectfully report that it i.s an inflexible
rule of this Grand Lodge not to interfere or meddle with political or religious matters:
at home or abroad. Its members may represent all shades of political and reljgioos
opinions, but when they are assembled in subordinate or Grand Lodge, they cannot
so much as discuss such opinions. Masonry has its own proper objects and purposes,
and those must be considered by us to the absolute exclusion of all others, and par·
ticularly of such as would certainly arouse contention and confusion. Of religion
we only desire to know that each one asking admission Is a sincere believer in God
and a future existence. Of politics we only ask if the applicant is a good citizen.
These questions are determined before his admission. Once admitted, all discusEion and consideration of religious and political affairs is strictly prohibited. As
individuals, doubtless, many of the members of this Grand Lodge feel a deep
Interest in the success of the struggle for independence in Cuba, and would be very
glad to do anything in their power to assist in securing the establishment and recognitk>n of that independence ; bot not one of them would be willing that the Grand
Lodge should in any way interfere, or so much as entertain a proposition for interference. Your committee are of opinion that this Grand Lodge should take no action
in the premises.

whenever there are three chartered Lodges in any State or Territory in which no

Grand Lodge has been established, those Lodges have the absolute right to meet In
Convention and organize a Grand Lodge for snch St.ate or Territory; that when a
Grand Lodge is once regalarly established in any State or Territory, It has exclusive
jurisdiction over all Mlleonlc Lodges and Masons within such State or Territory ; and
that no other Grand Lodge or Grand Body can establish a new Lodge within the territorial jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge so organized, or can maintain jurisdiction
over a Lodge therein to which It may have granted a charter. From the moment of
the organization of the new Grand Lodge its jurisdiction becomes absolute over the
entire territory, and all Lodges and all Masons there must acknowledge it and yield
-0bedience to it, and their allegiance elsewhere ceases. That we recognize as the law
here, bnt it is not recognized everywhere, and, as we understand it, the Grand
Lodges of England, Ireland, and Scotland claim and exercise the right of establishing
new Lodges in any part of the United Kingdom and ltt! dependencies, and the right
to maintain such Lodges under their obedience at ihetr pleasure.
,
We expect that foreign Grand Lodges and Grand Bodies will respect our rights,
and wi.11 not in any way interfere with the exclusive territorial jurisdiction of our
Grand Lodges, and we are <iulte willing to respect their rights in return. With
regard to jurisdiction, they must make the law for themaelves, as we .ha.ve made it
. for ourselves. If they are satisfied with a concurrent jurisdiction we cannot compla.i.n. and we will not knowingly tresp688 thereupon.
When Lodges owing allegiance to one or more foreign Grand Lodges unite in true
fot'mation of a Grand Lodge, as in Prince Edward Island or the Province of Manitoba, we recogniY.e the right of the mother Grand Lodges to maintain jurisdiction
over their own subordinates, and the duty of the subordinates to obtain consent
before severing their allegiance. .
Thie Grand Lodge would urge upon the mother Grand Lodges the propriety of
giving consent that their subordinates might in all proper ce.ees join in the eeta.bliehment of new Grand Lodges, and. whenever suoh consent is given, will be most
ha.ppy to recognize and enter into friendly relations with the newly established
Bodies•. In the judgment of y1>ur committee the best interests of Masonry will

The relation which this Grand Lodge maintains toward the Grand Lodge of Ham·
burg and the Grand Orient of France, to whom this "final appeal " is about to
be made, is expressed in our Standing Regulations now numbered 2 and 12. These
Regulations prohibit Masonic intercourse between tM Lodges and Masons of this
jurisdiction and those acknowledging allegiance to either of those offending Grand
LOdges-Hambnrg and France. Before these regulations were adopted-the first in
1865, $he second in 1869-every argument and appeal was exhausted in the vain
endeavor to persuade our trans-atlantlc brethren tliat they made war upon well
established and cherished law and custom on this continent ; but, instead of inducing
them to respect these laws and customs, which establish and regulate the jurlsdic·
tional rights of our Grand Lodges, they seem to have become more determiued in ·
their expressions of disregard and contempt for what we assert to be and insist upon
as our rights. Indeed, as if France borrowed the German idea, the former takes np
it and !orces into the discussion of the real question, in the same disingenuous spirit,
an issue refinedly unkind, which issue. cannot alarm any intelligent Mason who will
take pains to acquaint himself with Masonic law.
· The original acts complained of and protested against-the establishment of socalled Lodges within the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodges of New York and New
Jersey by the Grand Lodge of Hamburg, and the recognition of clandestine Lodges
within the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of Louisiana by the Grand Orient of
France-were not only not revoked, bnt their action was maintained as right, and the
offense has been renewed with an apparently settled unfriendly purpose to harass us
iu onr government, if such was possible, and in stolid indi.lference to the continuance
or existence of mntnal friendly relations.
To re-open the question and repeat the story would swell the volume of our
report _beyond any necessity, and accomplish.no good that we can anticipate. The
r ecords of the prominent Grand Lodges of the United States, from the year 1852 to
the present time, and especially of the Grand Lodge of New York, which was directly
assailed, tell the story amply and fully of the hostile and unfriendly acts of the
Grand Lodge of Hamburg; and commencing with the year 1868, when the threat;..
ened and premeditated acts culminated, the same record is found against the Grand
Orient of France. ·
If, to re-open the question, a reasonable prospect was promised of adjusting the
difficulties, we would gladly join with our Virginia brethren in the appeal, for we
are pained at the position in which some German and French brethren are placed
. who visit our country. To them these questions cannot be folly explained, and, •
unfortunately, when they arrive here they discover that they have had placed upon
them by their own Grand Lodges conditions which make them outcasts. We consider the question . closed and that the relation established between the Grand
Lodge of Hamburg and the Grand Orient of France, on the one side, and the Grand
Lodges of our Continent on the other, that of the aggressor and the aggrieved ; &nd,
so long as they oontinue this invasion, we must continue the use of every proper
weapon of defense which Masonic law and custom justifies.
With high respect for the fraternal and magnanimous sentiments by which the
Grand Lodge of Virginia has been actuated, we respectfully recommend that this
Grand Lodge do not unite in the appeal, and that it take no further action in the
matter until reparation has been ma.de to the satisfaction of the Grand Lodges of
New York, Louisiana, and New Jersey, and the invasion complained of has ceased.

The hour for the special order having arrived, the Grand Orat.or
the w.·. HENRY HUNTCiEY HAIGHT, late Governor of California, deliv~

1 cannot begin m,r address, in justice to myself and to you, without a truthfol
statement by way of apology. After having excused myself verb.ally and in writing
from the fulfillment of this duty, considering it impossible, in the midst of distracting
ca~es and engrossing busineea, to devote any time to its discharge, it was only yesterday morning, upon being informed by the Most Worshipfnl Grand Master that no
excuse would be received and that. a lame performance would be accepted rather
than none, that I seriously contemplated making my appearance before you in this
capacity. When you consider therefore that I am here under this mandate, with no
each leisure as I would have desired to prepare an address, you will doubtless, in the
true spirit of the fraternity, accept the will for the deed and be less disposed to
criticise.
It has alwayli been a favorite maxim of mine that no one should open his month
in public except to say, or at least to endeavor to say, something tending in some
way to the permanent good of his auditory. To communicate or recall some Interesting fact of science or history ,-to develop and impress some valuable principle
of government, of morals, or of religion-to atford, if possible, some aid to such as are
Inclined to pursue tile higher and nobler ends of existence,-theee seem to be the
legitimate purposes of public speaking. There seems to be 11 peculiar responsibility
in this regard resting upon those who are now and here on these shores laying the
foundations of what will be one of the greatest empires that ever rose under human
hands, and that will exhibit, we hope and trust, one of the grandest and most benefl.cent developments of either Hebrew or Christian civilization. Let any man cast his
eye forward a few short years-one quarter of a century-about the time that has
already elapsed since the discovery of gold in this State. Consider the etrect of the
completion of four lines of railroad across the continent, the great increase of popo·
lation In the United States, the accelerating volume of European immigration, our
growing commercial relations with Eastern Asia, the resistless progress of new ideas
in China and Japan, and the vast undeveloped resources of those nations for commerce and ~aterial contributions to the wealth of the world, especially in iron and
coal-and wlio can exaggerate the future of this coast or measure accurately the
changes of even oue short period of twenty-five years 7 Who can estimate the tre
mendoos lnfiuence op on the intellect of China aud Japan whkh most be exerted by this
close coot.act with the most active, free, and enterprising people of modern times 7
The theme I have chosen, however, for some random observations before this
august assemblage, is not the present or the_futore, bot the past. The idea of antiq·
uity is naturally suggested by one of the oldest of human organizations, and this idea
I will briefly attempt to develop. In the principal libraries of the world are stored
the chronicles of by-gone ages, the results of the experience of mankind in ancient
times, the record of the world's progress in the ch1ldhood and youth of the race, and
of those deeds of heroism and self-sacrifice the value of which, as a perpetual exam·
pie, are above all estimation. The love of things that are old, the passion for the
antique, the charm of antiquity, the fascination which the chronicles of the olden
times possess, are felt by most of us, and yet there are many who, if called upon,
could hardly, without retlection, account fully for the influence which these feelings
exert.
If a man were to sit down in 11 prosaic spirit and undertake to analyze this f'eel·
ing, to disease it logically, and to inquire into the rationale of it, he might easily
make out something of a case against It, and against himself for cherishing it.

Th~t there is In It mnch of what we term sent-h;.ent, and sometimes not a little affectation, ma! be conceded. .A blind reverence for antiquity is not rational. The
single qnahty of age has in it nothing specially admirable or attractive, apart from
other elements. In reasoning philosophically upon the subject it might be discovered that much of onr r_everence for the past Is mere sentimentalism, and not the
sober deduction of Intelligent reflection. If we were to be perfectly frank we might
find onrs.elves compelled to confess that many of our ideas of the past are about as
true to hfe as the castles in the air which boarding-school girls and college boys
·
constrnot and people with the heroes and heroines of fancy.
. Th~~e are two classes of people,-oue class conservative In morals, in religion,
m politic~, attached to the settled order of things, to established usage and prece·
de.nt, to t1m~-honored Institutions, reverenciqg the works, the opinions and the mero.ones of their fathers, venerating the wisdom of the past, and distrustful of experlm~nt and change-and there is another clsss which is restless of the old order of
things, radica~ in all things, progressive, sometimes perhaps more than is prudent,
fond ?' exp~r1ment, and strongly inclined to pervert the apostolic Injunction and try
all ~hmgs without holding fast to anything, good or bad. But even the latter class
while sometimes inclined to be destructive in government and to undervalue th;
lessons of experience, is not altogether without the universal love for antiquity.
In. the genuine antiquarian this passion manifests itself in an exaggerated degree.
To htm the most worthless trifle that has gained a few centuries of age becomes
prlc~Iess. A coin, a vessel or implement, one or two thousand years old possesses
to h'.m a value which money could not measure. He regards with ven~ration the
grani~e cliffs upon which have beaten the storms of centuries, and which have seen
the ~trth and death of unnumbered generations. Even in this democratic country
and m on~ modern mushroom society, there is not lacking the same peculiarity.

History deals with great characters, with leading facts, and fundamental princ'•
pies. It records the public acts of great men and the prominent features of great
epochs. It has little or nothing to do with the de~ils of private life, the foibles,
weaknesses, and small vices of its characters, or the daily uninteresting routine of.
household life and business cares and duties. It has to do with·national rather than
individual concerns. If it descended to the unromantic facts of daily life, we might
perhaps discover as mnch that is artificial, h ollow, and blast in the ancients as in the
painted and gilded specimens of modern fashionable society. The popular idea,
however, of the olden time, and of the men and women of that time, Is that the
world was then fresh and young, and that mankind partook of the unaft'ected youth
and freshness of civilization In its early dawn.
Our -v:iew of the scenes and chancters of past sges is mellowed by time ; the

and beauty of color and by their strange fadclnations afford us perpetual delight?
Man has a two-fold nature-physical and spiritual. There is a universal admiration for physical perfection, even among the most cultivated and intellectual. The
crlteiion of excellence and the test of superiority, in feudal times, was a somewhat
different one from that which is recognized in modern days. Then, bodily strength,
skill In the use of weapons, and personal prowess gave a man his pre-eminence over
the mass. The physical plays a much less Important part in modern times. The
present is an age of intellectual triumphs. The knights of the days of chivalry were
often unable to write their own names. .A.t the present day the ascendency. of mind
is recognized, but we moderns may be in as great danger of neglecting the body as
our ancestors were of negl_ecting mental culture.
If we were asked what we admire most about the men of feudal times, probably
we would specify their perfection In physical exerclHes, their feats of arms, and their
personal strengt.h and agility. The human form was developed by severe bodily
exercise and training, by a life in the open air, before the era of air-tight stoves, hotr
air furnaces, fancy dances at midnight, French cookery, tight lacing, tobacco and
drugged liquor. It is extremely donbtful whether, in the olden time, whatever other
excesses were committed, any considerable number of sane young ladies in respectable society could be found to start at ten o'clock at night to an entertainment,
dance all night, eat a supper after midniglft, aod--return home to bed about sunrise•
Of all social customs, this practice of turning night· into day seems most senseless
and Injurious.
Man has his various periods of physical development, from helpless infancy,
through buoyant youth aud the vigor of manhood, to the infirmities and decay of old
age. In this regard there is a singular parallel between national and individual life.
.All great nations, like men, have their periods of Infancy and yonth, of maturity and
decrepitude. The great empires of ancient times have furnished many striking
examples of this, and in the middle ages and in modern times snch instances have
not been wanting. Nations and races, like individuals, have had their origin, their
growth and culmination, their decline and fall. Success has commonly paralyzed
their energies, wealth and luxury enfeebled and enervated, and excessive effort
exhausted their strength, and the children, forgetting the virtues and losing the

To the M.·. W.·. Grand Lodge of California:The Committee on Jurisprudence have examined all the documents placed in
their hands, relative to the Grand Orient of Egypt, and report that they find therefrom,
and from other authentic sources, that a Grand Ma.sonic Body nnder the name of the
Supreme Oriental <;onncil was organized in Egypt in the year 1864: The name was
changed to that of Egyptian Orient in 1867. In 1872, the seat of this Grand Orient
. was fixed at the City of Alexandria, Wld on the twenty.first day of. Much, ltii7!l, U

Procee<lirigs of the

[Oct. 16,

was reorgRnized and assumed the name of the Grand Orient of Egypt, the Ill.·. Bro.
S. A. Zou being then elected and still continuing to be the Grand Master of the
Order in that Grand Orient.At the date of the reorganization there were a considerable number of Lodges
in Egypt working under charters issued by Grand Orients and Grand Lodges of Italy,
France, Germany, England, and America. This fact makes it manifest that a
Supreme Masonic authority and government was needed there. No one could doubt
the propriety of establishing a Grand Body which might receive such authority. The
Grand Orient of Egypt was established, and, so far as we can judge, upon a firm
basis, and not only with the permission, but under the proteotion and with the aotive
co-operation of the present Ruler of that country.
· In 1874 the representatives of nine Lodges, of which five were subordinates of
the Grand Orient of Italy, and three of the Grand Orient and one of the S11preme
Council of France, met in convention and issned a circular to all the Grand Lodges
and Grand Orients, protesting against the recognition of the Grand Oriem of Egypt
and denouncing it as irregular. The charges made in the circular are frivolous, and,
so far as we are advised, have received no attention from any Grand Body.
Among other things it is charged that this Grand Orient practices , the rite of
Memphis and has conferred degrees out of the regular order. We only know of the
rite of Memphis that it is recognized as a Masonic rite, as well as the Scottish rite
and the York rite, and that the degrees of Entered Apprentice, Fellow Craft; and
Master Mason are substantially the same in all these rites. Beyond those degree\
we do not inquire, nor do we care to know the meaning of the cabalistic signs and
figures used by those who practice those rites. We notice that the dignitaries of
Grand Bodies of the t:lcottlsh rite nse the figures "33° " after their names, and that
Grand Master ZOLA uses "33°" and" 96°-" We presume that these figures express
his rank or grade In the Scottish rite and in the rite of Memphis, and care little to
know whether our presumption may or may not be correct.
The Grand Orient of Egypt does not seek to subject to its obedience Lodges
owing allegiance to other Grand Bodies, and apparently pursues its own work quietly
and successfully. Your committee therefore propose and recommend the adoption
of the following resolution :Beaoltied, That the Grand Lodge of California recognizes the Grand Orient of
Egypt as a jnat and legally constituted Masonic Power.

Br~. WILLIAM A. DAVIES, from the same committee, presented the
followmg report :To the M.-. W.·. Grand Lodge of Oalifornia :Your committee have considered that portion of the Grand Master's Address in
1874, concerning our system of Inepectorehips, and cordially indorse his approval
of the successful results of the system, together with his dissent from the proposition made at the preceding Oommnnication-reqniring Inspectors to visit" only such
Lodges as have not been visited during the past year "-believing with him that no
reetrictio~ eho~ld be placed upon the plan of annual visitation, but rather leaving it
to the d1scret1on of the Inspector as to the necessity of an annual or even semiannual visit. Onr experience teaches us that, even in this jurisdiction, there exist
Lodges t.o which an Inspector's visit might be beneficial even more than twice a
year;_ and, from onr knowledge of the brethren who are devoting their time and
energies to the perfectiog of and insuring a uniformity in our Masonic work, we are
not prepared to believe that they, or any of them, would inftict an official visit
upon an unwilling Lodge, or when no necessity existed for such visitation.
In regard to the suggestion of the Grand Master to add to the title of Iospector
that of" District Deputy Grand Master," we do not think the change demanded
by reason of any important benefit 1o be derived therefrom, and are inclined to
believe that, by making frequent changes in our regulations concerning these matters, we are bnrthoning oor system with amendments which may endanger its perpe·
tnity. We would avoid any act tending to such a result, for while we yield our tribute
of praise to the nn·rewal'ded labors or our brethren-the Inspectors of our several
Masonic districts-we would not imperil the system so prodnctive of gpod results even
to accomplish the pleasing duty of rewarding those laborers with a more sonorous
title. From those members of the Grand Lodge whose experience dates back beyond
186.'i-the year in which our work was adopted and made obligatory upon the
Lodges-we know that we shall meet with an affirmative and ready response to the
declaration that the Grand Lodge of California has accomplished a great work, more
than it hoped to accomplish when its committee was appointed, and more than even
that committee, in its enthnaia;tic devotion to the business in hand, believed could
be accomplished.
It was the desire of the early mo,-ere in. the proposal to .attain uniformity in this
jurisdiction that, in certain requirements, the law should be absolute and should admit.
of but one interpretation. We were Masone from all parts of the world. fo the
same Lodge would be found a Master from Mississippi, a 8enior Warden from Maine, ·
a Junior Warden from Ohio, and a Senior Deacon from New York. · With no standard for a guide we were left at the mercy of their divers imaginings. Our Lodgeso
were " opened on the centre" in one locality, in another "on the square," and
in a third they were " declared " open. Our forms and ceremonies were represented and elaborated in as many different methods. The committee aimed to
present the simple plan which they believed would accomplish the result desired,
by first resolving that !>DI" Lodges should be opened and closed alike, and that
perfect uniformity should exist in our obligations and modes of recognition. Thie JOU ~ •
and much more we have attained, and our present perfect system is the result. We
·1 r
have done well-much better than we hoped for ten years ago-and we would not
endanger the encceee already reached by engrafting upon it any unnecessary
requirement.

Bro. GILBERT B. CLAIBORNE, from a majority of the Committee on
Jurisprudence, presented the following report:To the M. •. W. •• Grand Lodge of California:'Your committee have considered that portion of the Grand Master's Address
which cites the case of a member of a Lodge whose does being paid in fnll, made
application to his Lodge for 11" dlmit,'' and upon the application the Lodge granted
him a "certificate of withdrawal without rec1>mm&ndation." The brother refused to
accept the certificaie, 1111ying that it was not what he wanted. The Lodge declined
to grant him a recommendatory certificate, >&nd he was placed on the llst of members
withdrawn from the Lodge. Upon a representation of these facts the Grand Master
"decided that when the brother asked for a dimit he wanted a rec1>mmendatory
certificate of withdrawal, which alone wonld enable him to affiliate with another
Lodge," and further, that refusal to grant what is alleged to have been asked for,
did not interf&re with his standing, and that he was still a member of his Lodge.
Am1>ng other ways provided for separating from a Lodge, the third subdivision of
Seo. Ii, Art. I, Part V, of the Constitution, declares that membership is terminated
by voluntarily withdrawing therefrom after proper notice given. Section 6,'imme·
diately following, provides further that the member most be in good standing, his
does most be paid, and notice of his intention most be 'given at a stated -meeting.
This is all we can discover in the Constitution regulating the matter of volnnt.ary
termination of membership in a Lodge. The case presented by the Grand Master
does not fol fill the reqolrment of the law literally and technically, and if the brother
claims this adv.antage, and the Master 1>r the Lodge neglected at the time to require
him to c1>mply with the conditions laid down, it is evident that the proceeding was
informal, and neither the brother or the Lodge have changed their mntoal relations.
If the brother, being in good st.anding and his does being paid, had given notice at
a stated meeting of the Lodge of his intention to withdraw, we are of the opinion
that his membership would certainly have ceased at that meeting, unless there was
a reconsideration before it closed ; and this is all the law we can discover which
governs the matter and directs how membership may be voluntarily terminated.
What the brother meant in his application for a "dimit" this committee are not
prepared to say that they -clearly understand. The Word is used once in the Consti·
tntion, in Seo. 13, Art. III, Part III, which provides that no Lodge shall receive an
application for affiliation unless it be accompanied by a "proper dimit" from the
Lodge of which he was last a member, etc. After the act of withdrawal, it is oos.
~mary and proper to issue to a brother a paper, under seal of the Lodge, showing
his release. This paper has been entitled in several ways :-dimit, recommendatory
certificate, and cllrl.VitJate of urithdrawal without recommendation. The last two are
recognized by our Constitution and forms have been provided therefor, and if the
word " dimit '' is used as 11 title, we most understand it to mean either 1>f these
documents. The "recommendatory certificate " can not be given except by the
vote of a majority of the members of the L1>dge-see Sec. 6, Art. I, Part V-and so

ft would seem that it was intended as an honorarium, to be granted by the Lodge
only to those who win the favor by their singular merit and zeal for the welfare of

ip.embership, is issued by the Secretary of the Lodge nnder its seal by virtue of
his office, and is nothing more or less in fact than 11 certified copy of the record. It
contains no recommendation and is the simple evid~nce that the Lodge of which he
was last a member has no claim upon him floancially !Ir officially,.and we believe it
a pp.roach es nearest in its ch.a.1;11cter to the ancient and original cos tom. We are of the

to enable a br_other to affiliate with another Lodge, if the brethren who constitute

Bro. CHA,BL:&S L.'Wxoom, from a special committee, present.ad.the
following report :To the .M.". w... Grand Lodge of. Califomia:Yonr committee, appointed by the M.". W.". Grand Master, In accordance with a.
reeolntion adopted at the last Annual Communication, to make a'b investlgo.t.ioa of the
financial affairs of the Grand Lodge " and to 11nggll!it such reforms or Qkanges in the
matter of expenses as they may deem proper," have attended to the duties assigned
them and report as follows:They have carefully examined the expendltnres of the Grand Lodge for the last
ten yea.rs, and find that the principal items of expense are for salaries of Grand
Officers, for printing, for payment of representatives, and for appropriatio~ to the
various Boards of Relief.
Your committee believe that the amount paid as salaries to the Grand Officers is
no more than a fair compensation for the services rendered by them, and they cannot lu justice recommend a reduction thereof.
In the Item of printing, a reductlon might be m11de by omitting In the proceedi~a
the names of the members of the subordinate Lodges, but the small amount to be
g.iined by this omission would be no eqnivalent for the Joss to the Craft of so ~oi:iv11nlent and useful a source of iuformation.
The Reports on Correspondence might be a.bridged or omitted, but this would
.acarcely comport with the dig~ity of the Grand Lodge, for in these report.a the
