Procredings.of the

[Oct. 16,

Maaonia Intelligence from every qnarter of the globe le col!Rted and dietribnted, not
only to the members of the Order, bnt to all who choose to read them.
Tbe price paid for printing Is reduced to the lowest figure possible, and the work
cannot be done for less than the amount now charged therefor.
With regard to the donations annually made to tbe various Masonic Boards of
Relief, amonnting in the aggregate, last year, to the sum of $2500, yonr committee
are of the opinion that, in the question of the reduction of expenses, the last item to
be considered should be that which would close the treasnry against the sacred
appeals of charity; bnt, as the amount tbns donated forms a very considerable item
in the expenditures of the Grand Lodge, your committee desire, without snggestion,
to call the attention of the Grand Lodge to the matter and leave it to the discretion
of ite members whether the appropriations should be continued or withheld.
With reference to the representative fond, a saving may be made by the adoption
of a resolution declaring that no Lodge shall receive from that fond an amount
larger than tha.t contributed by it. By this means the som of one thousand three
hundred and thirty-four dollars would be aonoally saved to the Grand Lodge, and
one hundred and thirteen Lodges wonld be pecnniarily benefited thereby, while
eighty-five Lodges would be obliged to pay a portion of the expenses of their representatlve.s from their own funds. Whether it would be wise to retrench in tbis
manner your committee express no opinion, bot present the matter for the consider&·
tion of the Grand Lodge.
The Grand Lodge is tbe possessor of 1318 shares of the stock of the Masonic Hall
Association, of the par value of thirteen thousand one hundred and eighty dollars;
and, as the debt upon the property is now reduced to forty thousand dollars, the
dividends upon this stock will soon be available to aid in defraying the cn1Tent
expenses of this Grand Body.
The contingent expenses of the Grand Lodge, for rent of offices, stationery,
painting portraits of Past Grand Masters, printing diplomas, binding proceedings of
other Grand Bodies for the library, purchase of books for the same, &c., your committee think cannot well be reduced witb a dne regard to the interests of tbe Grand
Lodge.

The Grand Master then delivered his Annual Address to the Grand
Lodge, as follows :BRETHREN OF THE GRAND LoDGE OF CALIFORNIA:The revolving year occasions our accustomed assemblage to be attended with
a peculiarity of circomete.oce never to have repetition in oar individual existence.
"We witness the end of orie century and the commencement of e.uother-the old and
the new encountering and jostling each otlier-the one retreating with its realized
past, the other advancing with its problematical future. .
One hundred years ago the Federal Convention which framed the.Constitution, and
the Continental Congress which proclaimed the Declaration, were composed of men
who, with few exceptions, were Freemasons. When reiterated oppression had
exhausted the patience of submission, when repeated solicitation for amelioration
and iedrese were unheeded or answered by severer and other impositions, when
the devotion of loyalty was unr~cognized and unrewarded, then, and then only, did
these men, nnited.in a bond of brotherhoo.d -a onion founded for the relief of mankind-set forth the principles of liberty and eqnality; liberty which required the
protection of intelligence and organization, and eqne.lity given by changing loyalty
into patriotism, a compelled transfer of allegiance from the king to the people: and
to the maintenance of these principles were pledged their lives, their fortunes, and
their sacred honor.
These brethren, founders or a nation, representing the nobleet,sentlmente in their
sympathy with popnlar snfferings, with no motive eave that of fidelity to honest con· .
viction, by the example of patient effort and unremitting sacrifice and an immovable'
and ~ee.ntifol fe.itb, me.de their followers noyieldiog to discouragement or defeat, and

In the retr~spect of the past oentnry it would seem that no nation has been more
greatly intrusted with destinies which have had universal inllnence, or has more folly .
realized "that grand progress which is bearing hnmanity onwards to a higher intelligence and a no bier character." The march of progress has been noted for the in· .
crease of population and area, the extension of agriculture by force of immigration,
the enlargement of foreign and domestic commerce, mechanical invention and multi·
plication of industries, immense products and marvelous mineral resonrces, wondrons
discoverles In science, the application of steam and electricity, the cultivation of the
fine aria and literature, the advancement in law, medicine, philosophy, social science,
and improvement in every form, the higher standard of education, reformatory
schemes for a socceSl!fol contest with social mischief, the establishment of special
institutions for the relief of a!Hiction in its particular forme, and the organization of a •
variety of societies for charitable porPQses, wutoal aid and protection, and for the
enhancement and refinement of common life. These achievements are promin.ent
tests of a higher and more complete civilization. Sorely, it has been a century of
development without parallel.
During this period Freemasonry has had an onward , though checkered, course.
The itinerant Lodges of the Revolutionary Army, and the few isolated Lodges of particular localities, have been succeeded by Grand Lodges with nearly nine thousand ·
subordinates; members who were limited to hundreds in number, are now counted
by hnndreds· of thousands; and the humbl\l Lodge-rooms have been supplanted
by edifices oonspicooos for architectural beauty and grandeur. For a. brief period
fanaticism, hate, and intolerance created a wild anti-Ma.sonic excitement in certain
sections with a party that called for the censure and condemnation ol Masons; nay,
further, for their proscription and exclusion from public office or trust. Bending, not
breaking, to the gale which raged with an almost uncontrollable fury , always on
guard against menace and peril from without, denounced by church and persecuted
by communities, our noble brotherhood awaited the return of reason, firm in the.
belief that trnth in the end would assert itself, and that it would come forth from
the storru, crippled perhaps, bot more firmly united by bonds made closer by danger
and solfering; and it was borne by an even current to a prosperity not imagined and
without precedent.

One bas been of general preovalence.f I have reference to the lack of attendance at
Lodge meetings. Many apparently believe that, without an official position, there is

Then come the dronish or holiday Ma.sons, ever on the alert to enjoy a right or

Another class would attend were the workings of the Lodge made more attractive,
and this leads directly to the many times repeated recommendation that greater care
be taken in the selection of officers, and that those officers be ever active and
efficient in duty and affable and considerate in their relation11 with the brethten.
That one is simply a favorite by reason of being a good fellow, in c.1mmon parlance,
is sµrely no qualification in itself for the Important position of Master, bot dignity,
excellence, and intelligence are essential requisites, combined with a calm and judicial
temper. Masters ought to have enough knowledge of the work and lectures to claim
and attract attention, and be conversant enough with law and parliamentary usage to
have their rulings properly respected and cheerfully obeyed. I wonld have every
Master so well acquainted with his duties that the very feeling of_being right will constitute power, and then the brethren, impreaaed by his knowledge, will be willing to
yield a ready obedience. Masters must be Masters in their work of administration, but
in the exerci~e of authority the rights of the governed are to be heeded and protected,
and the authority is to be acknowledged and not arrogantly displayed. Responsibilities will be met and confidently treated, if the assurance of being correct comes
from sound reasoning, derived from & complete acquaintance with the subject con
sidered. Masters, to receive the respect of others, must so act that they can honestly
respect tbemselvel!-not only practicing the greater, bot the lesser virtues-those
amenities which society expec.ts and the gentle in manner perform, and in the exercise
of command they should be mindful that to master one's self is the first condition of
healthy thought and acti~
While I make no apology for the brother who can but will not frequent bis Lodge,
I do understand and am charitable enough to consider some of the pleas valid which

Grand Lodge of California.

1876.]

are set forth in explanation for his absence. There is an excuse given for non-attendance which is substantial, and is found in the imperfect ventiltltion of the Lodge.
room. It is urged, with troth, that not only physical inconvenience, but actual
illness, is often ·produced by confinement in a Lodge-room surcharged with heated
and vtti_ated air, and that for comfort and health it is better to remain away.
Hygiene is sufficiently popularized to make self-evident the necessity for thorough
ventilation, and to avoid the deleterious consequences of inspiring air which bas been
contaminated by the respiration of many persons. It teaches that confined air, under
all circumstances, is injurious if inhaled Into the longs-air, like water, requiring to
be kept in motion to be retained in a condition fit to enter the system. In visiting
:Masonic halls In many portions of the State, my attention bas been directed, by personal discomfort, to the insnfficient arrangements, in their construction, for proper
ventilation. Balls, new and old, however eligibly located or lllltisfactorilly eqnlpped,
are, with very few exceptions, most unhappily deficient in this essential. My observation and experience warrants the declaration that no inconsiderable percentsge
of illness among the brethren may be traced as having origin directly or resulting
from the impure ventilation of defective Lodge-rooms; and the original illness has
sometimes caused a chronic disease terminating in death. Others will doubtless
corroborate the correctness of the assertion, and to them, at least, it will not be
surprising that brethren will absent themselves, especially iu those districts where,
during the heated term, ill-ventilated apartments are almost insupportable.
It is not only my duty, but I consi<ier it fit to call your attention to this subject,
confident of its importance and hopeful that it will awaken investigation as to the
means to be employed in removing existing defects, and will make it imperative, In the
building of futnre Masonic Balls, for the architect to insure perfect ventilation.
Much of the discord which at times unfortunately is found in Lodges, and mnch of
the opprobrium cast by the outer world upon our Order, can be traced, without
deviation, to the too common practice of receiving improper material into our community. This injury, which is constantly perpetrated, occasions more serious results
in its effect upon the position, estimation, and propagation of Masonry than have the
anathemas of Rome, or revilement or persecution from whatever source or extent.
The standard of qualification is too often departed from, either from hasty acceptation, careless investigation of character, or the mistaken policy of seeking quantity
rather than quality. It bas happened that a paucity of funds in the treasury bas
caused a lenity that otherwise would not pertain, contrary to the rigor that ought
always to have enforcement. Again, it should be remembered that there are other
objects sought to be attained by our institution besides making Masons, which is too
commonly regarded as the main object. Candidates ought to possess positive, not
negative, traits and be ·estimated for the good done rather than the evil avoided. As
Jong as these causes exist, the effect will continue ; but conld this noxious element be
removed, no greater advantage could be acquired. Every Lodge is responsible to the
Fraternity for the quality of material furnished; it has the inspection and the shaping,
and if imperfections are discovered, the blame or acceptsnce rests with the Lodge.
~be remedy for this diseased condition will be found in the refnsal of the individual
brother, or the committee, to recommend until sufficient time or trouble is taken to
scrutinize reputation, ascertaining not only the recent bot the remote conduct of the
applicant; for there can be no excuse for any negligence or haste, and no permissible
avoidance of the duty, in every case which presents a doubt, to give the benefit of the
doubt to the Fraternity.

A. common cauRe of trouble is the tardy or non-payment of dues, the former producing pecuniary embarrassment, and the latter, at times, certain complications
Incident to the death of a suspended member. Jt would seem that a brother who

the consequences of suspension. Did this invariably occur, there would be no qnes·

and we will find that if the law be obeyed this cause of trouble will terminate.
What should be done with non-affiliates? This is a question which agitates the
Fraternity in this and other jurisdictions. Non-affiliation is a silent though potent
cause of injury to Lodges, by retarding growth, limiting action, and depressing ardor.
Non-affiliates are an inert mass, a barrier to the more perfect success of the Order;
and by very inaction they are stumbling-blocks in the way of the zealous, more detri·
mental in passivity than our enemies in activity. What, then, shall be the disposition
of these useless leaden weights? Conciliation is one method; legislation to compel,
under penalty of expulsion, is another. On principle I am in favor of abolishing the
affiliation.fee, that no financial impediment, however slight, may interpose· to hinder

a dilatory brother from returning to the Lodge, since by some its demand may be
regarded as inciting non-affiliation, (a sorry loophole Indeed,) while fr11nkly avowing
my belief that the moderate sum required would be no hindrance to the brother, if he
were really anxious to return.
In a lo~lityln this State there are two Lodges with a combined membership of Jess
than one hundred and eighty, where the number of the unaffiliated amount to nearly
two hundred. Here it iii evident that other causes besides the affiliation fee operate
against applyipg for admission. Even the proposed amendment to the Constitution
concerning the number of negative votes required, etc., to reject an applicant for
affiliation, apart from the provisions being antagonistic to.ancient Masonic Jaw, which
demands a unanimous consent for admission, and, in regarding tlie ballot as secret,
makes the secrecy inviolate, and all innovation to be discouraged, maintaining the
established and understood old, in preference to the doubtful and untried new, wonld
hardly smooth the way for the non-affiliate; for under the law he has only, in event of

and this w1thont the payment or any further dues. To legislate for compulsory affiliation, with a trial and penalty for its non-compliance, is in opposition to the accepted
doctrine of freedom in thonght and action, and it would not be difficu!t to conceive or
contemplate the results of such an attempt; still, exacting justice wonld warrant the

to the Lodge, since unwillingness, equally with indifference, is always injurious to successful prosecution; and if the forfeiture of the benefits of membership is without force
in inducing affiliation, the gain to be obtained from compulsion may well be questioned.
Difficully is experienced by many Lodges in collecting the present amount of dues,
yet I am convinced that commonly it wonld be for their ultimate welfare if the dues
were greater, for he who is able and wllling to pay is not likely to demur at the
increase. It certainly ls desirable for every Louge to have as nearly as possible a fixed
sour~e or revenne, and this can be arrived at only by membership dues.
A revenue
drawn from fees· for the degrees is uncertain, depending upon the amount of work
done, and this depends upon circumstances more or less accidental, so that as a
source it can not have a definite reliance. The usual expenses of a Lodge should be
µiet by funds derived from does, and wholly irrespective of that coming from fees,
thereby preventing any relaxation in the acceptance of candidates which might be
excited by a desire for the money obtained, rather than the character of the initiate.
Briefly, each Lodge, to be in a sound condition, vigorous and effective, must have a
treasury supplied from an absolute revenue, such as regular does, to which, if there
be added the fees, exemption will be secured from pecuniary embarrassment, the
Fr11ternity will be less liable to imposition, and, by an observer from without, the
genuineness of Masonry will have more ready acceptance.

Several questions were asked, having origin in a case presenting the following
facis:-A. brother, suspended by his Lodge for non-payment of dues, removed thirty
miles distant, where another Lodge was established. He was an honest, correct, hai'd·
working man,. laboring worthily to comfortably situate his family, and with intention

to ultimately pay his dues, he being "too proud" to ask for their remission. He was
accidentally injured, and immediately after, money was sent by a brother to pay the
delinquent does, which were received and receipted for by the Secretary. Three
honrs after the departure of the messenger with the money, and before it had been
paid, the injured brother died, which fact being made known to the Secretary, be,
by direction of the Master, returned the money with an explanation that reinstatement could not be obtained after death. As my decision was in opposition to one
rendered by a former Grand Master in an analagous case, and as it will not have the
concurrence of all, I crave your iudul!(ence to report it somewhat in detail.
To the several questions I replied that the suspended brother, having been a man
of integrity and morality, and by labor endeavoring to extricate him~elrfrom pecuniary difficulty and to comfortably establish his family, his condition ought to have
been favorably considered by his Lodge, his does remitted, or further time grantedbriefty, that be ought net to have been suspended; that he erred in not soliciting remission, it being the duty and the right of every distressed, worthy brother, bnt, moved
by a false pride, he sought for no remission nor farther time, was suspended, and iu
that condition continued until death; that the fact of the dues being paid and
receipted for, alter death, did not remove the suspension, for death precluded a reinstatement, and the action of the Secretary was performed under the impression that the
brother was alive, and consequently, in a strictly legal sense, the money having been
received erroneou@ly, the act of refunding made that of receiving null and void; that
my sympathy was in favor of the deceased brother, and that I would that the Lodge bad,
after having received the dues, ignored the fact of death having occurred before the
payment, and suffered the supposed reinstatement to have had the effect of actual
restoration, in consideration of his worth, the misfortune of suspension, and the condition of his widow and children; but that, as a decision was demanded, it had to be
framed in a·c cordance with the law' which clearly defines the act of suspension, its
consequences and means of removal, and was based upon the position that a suspended brother, when dead, cannot be reinstated.
In this case the conclusion would operate disadvantageoosly for those immediately
interested, yet genera.l ly its effect will be for the common good, for if a brother performs personal duties pertaining to dnes, and a Lodge has positive, satisfactory evidence of a member's situation before pronoanciug suspension, the law will be considered just, humane, and sufficiently complete to obviate any modification in its
construction.
To an inquiry made by an Inspector as to the propriety of giving a certificate of
qualification to a Master elect who, by reason of continued intoxication, was likely
to have his inetalhtion objected to, I replied, that if the Mw;ter elect should be found
qualified to give the work and lectures entire in the three degrees, he would be
entitled to receive the certificate. If, howevM, he conducted himself improperly,
whether by drunkenness ()I' other disqualirying action, it would be the duty of any
member of the Lodge to object to the installation, and to prevent the same, if necessary, by preferring charges; for, if a Master elect is thus censurable, so far forget• the
duty he owes to himself and his Lodge and the teachings inculcated on his initiation,
and is so destitute of moral force to control bimselr, it is obvious that he could not
govern others, or do "justice to the office which he would hold, to the brethren over
whom he would preside, and to the candidates whom he would be called to instruct."

not interested in the result of the trial, competency perhins; and, as the great object
of every trial is to elicit truth, and in the spirit of troth to administer justice, I could

I have been obliged in two instances to caution officers against the expenditure of

stalled officers, or to interest and draw brethren from their supioeneBB, or even to

of the Grand Lodge in 1873, making Lodges gather and hold their funds for the promotion of purposes strictly Masonic, with emphatic prohibition of any disbursement
not in accord with such purposes; and I directed that henceforth Lodge moneys must

responsible for the cost.

A dispensation for the forma.tion of a Lodge at Tucson City, Arizona Territory, has

in white gloves and aprons, with a sprig of acacia, and marching to the grave in procession, where the printed funeral service was read, the Kprig of acacia dropped, and

appeared unobjectionable, since the actin no way represented a Masonic organization,
legal or clandestine, but was simply the employment of a form of burial pecnliar to
Masonry, and in the instances cited, used by Masons only, who were actually deprived
of Lodge advantages; and I therefore expressed the opinion that the practice might be
continued until the establishment of a Lodge wonld render the same unnecessary and
unwarrantable, and that this opinion had the force of recognized precedents.

l~t. sad tnb~te of respect to his remains. As the long, mournful, silent procession
of kindred, friends; brothers, companions, Sir Knights, and representatives from other
organizations, conveyed the body through the streets to the church, and from church
to the grave, spectators, in witnessing the general grief and solemn honors could
have exclaimed," Over the tomb of such a man tears might fall, bot not one' could
be 11 tear of bitterness." We consigned our brother to his last resting place and felt
that his life, in it.a praiseworthy usefulness, was his eulogy, and should be measured

·~

Gramd Lodge of Oalifornia.

S57

by what it had accomplished rather than by its duration; that he would still live in
his good deeds, venerated memory, and fruitful example ; and that in devout repeti'
tion of his Master's words, he might have said, "I have finished the work which
Thou gavest me to do."
·
Another familiar face has disappeared. A few weeks since BENJAHIN HORTON
F~, in the vigor of ripened manhood, left for 11 visit to his childhood's home,
there to rejoin an invalid wife who had joyfully announced her convalescence. Prior
to his departure, in the fullness of happiness, in bright anticipation of a speedy meeting
with i\is love·d ones, as a friend has touchingly said, "to nee his own words, he
was as happy as he could wish to be, and thanked God fervently for all the blessings
he enjoyed." Alas, for human 11xpectatione ! ABl!ailed by an insidious disease he
resisted only to finally succumb, and the mournful tidings of his decease came unexpectedly to gloom the hearts of his many friends. Brother FREEHAN died in Canton,
Massachusetts, on the sixteenth day of the last month. He, also, was a pioneer,
and, during his long and prosperous career in this State, was closely allied with religions, political, aud benevolent associations. For five years as Master of California
Lodge, No. 1, and as a ·member and President of the Masonic Board of Relief of
San Francisco; po888ssed of an amiable quality of temper, cordial address, and sincerity of purpose and action, he gave earnest and valuable labors for the advance·
ment and prosperity of these institutions. His long and faithful attachment to the
Craft was acknowledged and rewarded by you in. sncceesively maJi:ing him Junior.
and Senior Grand Warden and Deputy Grand Master; and you know the fidelity with
which he filled these offices and discharged their important trusts. His habits were
simple, &ogal, and temperate. In the pursuit of the practical he employed thrift
and methodized life; upright and honest, he was a useful and respected citizen;
morally strong and religiously steadfast, he was devoted to the Fraternity, and in
adhering to its teachings and principles, he was a good Mason.
One year ago our brothers were with us; they are now gone, having solved lire's
mystery. May these repeated monitions make us mindful of the self-evident bot too
frequently repressed truth, that we are mortal, and make us aware of the inferiority
of earthly matters when compared to the immortality which, unknowable in life,
death alone reveals; so that in living closely to the practice of the good and the
trne, our words, our works, and oftr example may be so treasured in memory that
men shall say of us-·
"Glad souls without reproach or blot,
Who do God's will and know it not."
In this period· of political excitement, amid the strife, bitterness, and vituperation
allowed by an unbridled license to rival parties, when a mass of abuses and evils are
paraded, and we are daily informed of official oortnption, political selfishness, and
the cunning of men whose individual interests and vaulting ambit.ion are often promoted at the expense of pnblic welfare ; when we constantly witness the love of
wealth and the care for riches which infinence, and to some extent, regulate social
life, giving 11 blindness to moral good and undermining virtue and honesty, we may
rejoice that this assemblage is strictly due to a loyalty which rises above natural
selfishness-a loyalty without reserve in devotion, without recognition of creed or
party-11 loyalty to the never-ceasing cause of humanity, whiob, as embodied in our
organization, combines the practioal unselfishness of charity with the immutable
principles of trnth, justice, and purity.
'
Freemasonry, while it has always plBCed itself in hostile array against intolerance, dogmatism, and bigotry, Is ever in accord with the progressive spirit of the
age. Entertaining no views of impracticable and impossible conditions, it does not
pretend to settle quest.ions which agitate political and relitioos communities-its
actual mission being to preserve its own undeviating course. Men and actions are
judged with equanimity; moral Instructions are inculcated; and in Its very nature it

358

Proceedings if the

[Oct. 10,

is essentially in harmony with the declaration of n~tural and revealed religion.
Strong In the assertion of ita own trnth, it is the uncompromising enemy of falsehood; and, having nothing to defend in the past, it steadfastly adheres to a prescrihed
conrse, and in its vitality and durability sees nothing to fear in the future. It cherishes that which is good, troe, and right, awarding to each a proper valne, an<\ has
an ideal of social perfection, to the attainment of which It incites hlgh, ennobling
thonghta and a sense of moral responsibility, and thos in the enforcement of the
pure and the beautiful, prepares for the "life beyond life."
Brethren, I have DOW acquainted you with the most Important of the various
official acts of my administration. If in the message thereby formed a tone or egotism be detected, I ask your pardon ; and If it has not the merit of brevity, it has
the virtoe of truth, honestly told. In di~chargiog the honorable trost with which you
invested me, I have sought to perform the part of executive irrespective of personal
Influences; and in laboring for the common weal I have sought reward in your
approbation. Io surrendering authority, my acknowledgment is made with feelings
of gratitude and pleasure for the courtesy and assistance received &om the Grand ·
Secretary and other Grand Officers, and for the fraternal greetings and earnest welcome bestowed whenever and wherever I have met the Craft. I have, jndeed,
received the "generous support" assured to me by my immediate predecessor.
We are now ready to begin the bnsineee of the twenty-seventh Annual Commonicatioo. Let ns treat the questions which may be presented for deliberation with a
jodgmeut influenced by charity towards dissenting opinions; let ne exercise the
sweetness of sympathy, that discussion may not weaken the strength of harmony;
and as humble imitators of God's beneficent love to man, let us invoke His blessing
for guidance and direction.
JOHN MILLS BROWNE,
Grand Ma.atBr.

The Grand Lecturer presented his Annual Report ~o the Grand
Lodge, a.s follows;To the M. ·• W. •• Grand Lodge of California :In accordance with a regulation of this nrand Lodge, I submit the following report
of my official acts during the past year:Boon after the close of the last Annual Communication, namely, on the 25th day
of October last, I opened in this city a Lodge of Instruction and continued the same
ee.c~ Monday evening until the first Monday in December, thereby affording an opportumty for each officer, who desired it, to render himself proficient in the work.
I have issued certificates of qualification to t.he Masters elect of the following
Lodges, viz.: Nos. 1: 13, 14, 16, 22, 50, 84, 88, 120, 127, 136, U2, 151, 168, "191, 208,
211, 216, 21_9, 226, _287, and 240. All these, except four, were examined by myself;
the_exceptions being Nos. 13, 88, 219, and 237, who were examined, and their qualiflcat1on• vouched for, by brethren who were known to me to be proficient in .the work
and lectures.
.
I accompanied the Grand Master on his official visit3 to the following places, viz. :
San Jose, Santa Barbara, Ban Buenaventura, Los Angeles, Ban Bernardino Anaheim
Visalia, Santa Rosa, Healdsburg, Oakland, Sacramento, Dixon, St. Hele~a, Clover'.
dale, Lakeport, and sundry of the Lodges in this city. At ten of these places district
meetings were held, at which nearly all the officers of the Lodges comprised in the
several district3 were present. At these meetings instruction in the ritual was give n
in the morning and alternoon sessions, and the work was exemplified In the evenings
by the officers in attendance. In most cases the officers manifested a strong desite
to correct any irregularities pointed out to theiii, and to perfect· themselves in the
work. ·
The resolution passed at the last Annual Communication requiring Inspectors to
~rocnre the Grand Le.cture~'s certificate as to qualification, could not, I regret to say,
in all cages, be complied with. In some instances brethren, who were well known
tO me to be proficient in the work and lectures, declined t o serve as Inspectors
when tendered the position by the Grand Master. When the annual elections took
place in December last, and it became necessary for him to make the appointments, I
reluctantly issued sever&! certificates upon the recommendation of brethren who were
known to me to be proficient in the ·work, and who vouched for the correctness of
the work of the proposed Inspectors.
Reports have been received from thi,rteen districts, of which a more or less brief
synopsis is herewith presented.
Inspector JoHN A. WATSON, of the first district, visited all the Lodges under his
charge, except Crescent, No. 45. He reports them to be in good condition and doing
fair work.

ALABAMA.
The Grand Lodge of this jurisdiction commenced it~ fifty.fifth Annual Commnni·
cation in the city of Montgomery on the sixth day of December,1875,-tbe M.-. W.-.
ISJ.IJ.H A. WILBON, Grand Master, presiding, and the~... w. .. DANIEL SAYRE being
Grand Secretary. Representatives were present from one hundred and seventy-seven
Lodges.
The Grand Master's Address is rather brief, bot well written, and is mainly confined
to the Masonic business of the year. He congratnlates the Fraternity on the fact
that " the cause of Masonry has prospered in peace and nnity in the jurisdiction."
But death had been at :work and had taken from earth the M.-. W.·. ROBERT H. ERVIN,
a Past Grand Master, whu bad made bis mark for good among bis fellow-men and
Masons. We copy this deserved tribute to his memory:On the eleventh day of January, 1875, Past Grand Master ROBERT H. ERVIN departed this life calmly and sweetly, at bis home in Wilcox county. For many years
onr deceased brother devoted himself to the interests of Masonry- its advancement
and honor. He was ever at the post of duty with a willing hurt, a strong arm, and
a skillfnl hand. Bis devotion to the Mystic Art, bis experience in its arcana, and his
earnest activity in ditfusing its li!fbt, made him for years one of its principal supports
in this jurisdiction; while bis gemal nature, bis amiable disposition, and virtnons walk,
endeared him to all good men. He was a Mason, worthy of a Mason's r eward. How
mysterionP, that death should have selected him for a victim, in the vigor of manhood, in the strength of life, and in the midst of its active and useful duties. I feel
I am privileged to tender the deep sympathy and condolence of this Grand Lodge to
his greatly. bereaved family and friends, and to express the hope that when bis work
was called to pass the test of an unerring Square, it wns fonnd true and trusty, and
that our lamented brother bas left his sphere here to occupy a higher and more
glorious •phere in the Celestial Lodge. The long connection of our brother with
this Grand Lodge, the responsibl~ and exalted position he filled with so much credit
to himself and honor to the Fraternity, renders It proper that this Grand Lodge
should express its sense of this sad bereavement.
.
Five new Lodges had been constituted during the year. Of 'the many decisions
made by the Grand Master, we note the following as of general interest:A woman who has been divorced from her husband is not a competent witness
against him in a Masonic tribunal, as to matters or things which transpired during

covertnre, but would be competent as to matters occurring subsequently to the
divorce.
The written testimony used in a court of law or chancery, cannot be need as evidence in a Masonic trial, except by the conee11t of the parties thereto.
A judgment of a court of law, or a decree In. chancery, may be Introduced in a
Ji[asonic trial, simply for the purpose of showing that snch judgment or decree had
been rendered.
Citizens of this State, who have been improperly made Masons in another
jurisdiction, must be healed and pay the regular fees prescribed by our Constitution,
before they can be admitted to membership in any subordinate Lodge in this jurisdiction.
Neither of 'the first three officers of a subordinate Lodge can dimit during the
term of bis office.
Dueling is an offense against the moral law, as revealed in the " Great Light;" it
Is therefore a Masonic offense for which a brother Is amenable to such discipline as
the Lodge may see proper to inflict, even to expulsion from the Order.
A Mason's t\imily can have no .Masonic privileges, except through the Mason him·
self. Therefore, whe1' a Mason dies, being at the time under suspension for non-pay·
ment of dues, bis family cannot, after his death, pay up hJs does, and thereby restore
themselves to such Masonic Jlrivileges as they would have been entitled to if he bad
died in good standing in the Lodge.
No brother, if present, can be excused from voting upon the reception of a candidate ; and any brother persisting in a refusal to vote in such a case, renders himself Ifable, and charges should be preferred for a violation of bis obligation.
A Mason should not be prejudged nor subjected to any punishment until he has
been found guilty; therefore, a brother may visit and take part in the proceedings of
his Lodge, though "under charges," until a trial and conviction is had,
An Entered Apprentice Is not entitled to a dimit, but in case of bis removal from
the ~nrisdiction of the Lodge in which he was initiated, the Lodge may furnish him a
certificate, setting forth the fact of bis initiation.
They hllve a "Committee on Work" in Alabama, which exemplifies and t~aches
the same at the Atmual Communications; and at other times and places when
required. A proposition had been made to substitute a Grand Lecturer therefor.
To this the Grand Master is opposed, and gives several weighty reasons for his opin·
ion. In our own jurisdiction we have fonnd the Grand Lecturer and the Inspectors an
excellent institution for the promotion of uniformity in work.
We think that the Grand Lodge dealt ont some Masonic justice in one remark·
able case which was reported upon by its committee. .A. brother deserted his wife .
and married the daughter of a Master Mason. The fact of bis first wife being still
alive was brought to bis notice, but he persisted in repudiating her and living· with
the second; whereupon he was tried for the crime of adultery, and that with a
brother Master Mason's daughter and sister-for her brother was also a Master
Mason. His Lodge found him guilty as charged, bot refnsed even the pnnlsbment of
reprimand. 'l'he committee of the Grand Lodge characterized such action as it de·
served, and on its motion the offending brother was expelled from all the rights and
privileges of Masonry, and bis L odge was sev:erely reprimanded by the Grand Lodge.
The Grand Lodge of Utah was fraternally recognized, with an apology for the
seeming .neglect In not havjng done so before. Recognition of several other new

ARKANSAS.
The thirty-seventh Annual .Communication of the Grand Lodge of Arkansas was
commenced ·at Little Rock on the eleventh day of October, 1R75,-the M.·. W.·. M. L.
BELL, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.'. W.·. LUKE E. BARBER being Grand Secre·
tary. Representatives were present fr'>m sixty-eight Lodges.
The Address of Grand Master BELL Is well written, and is one of those docnments
that does one good not only to read bnt to study. We wonld make ample extracts
therefrom, for the benefit of our readers, had not J:lro. ABELL marked our C'>PY with
those forbidding hi61'oglyphics, "No duplicate.'' We will copy a gem or two. All
onr readers, we are a88nred, will be gratified to learn that the cloud which was
resting, politically and Masonioally, on Arkansas has, partially,at least, disappeared,
and tha.t glimpses of clear sky are seen in its plape. Here is what the Grand
Master says : Our beloved State has been, politically, in a feverish state of excitement and
uncertainty for fifteen years, and though no political ideas or discn88ions can find a
place in our sacred retreat, yet we are citizens of the State and have a large interest
in her welfare. We are taught to be loyal to the Government; but true loyalty can
only come from the heart, and no people can love their rulers or the Government
which does not bring them peace, prosperity, confidence and rest·-tb.at security
which is tb.e basis of hope. • • • • The late cl.vii war, and the political and
financial distress resulti1Jg from our late government, have retarded the.prosperity
of the State and depressed the hopes of our people to such an extent that our Fra·
ternity, feeling the general gloom , has not accompii&hed that material progress that
we conld have wished. At our last Communication onr people were just emerging
from a state of great political excitement. Every one was in sn~pense as to the
result in the near future; and, as if to still furthe1· depress the hopes of the people,
the crops had partially failed all over the State, and great distress and suffering were
severely. threatened in many commnnities. But how changed the prospect, now l
We ·have a 8tate Government founded upon the free choice of .a grateful people. All
are satisfied with it. If not the "best government the sun ever shone upon.'' it is
e.t least good enough for us, for we are happy and contented. What more can a
people ask? And, as if to 1111 our cup of blessing foll to overflowing, and to con·
'Vince us tb.at the darkest hour is just before day, a kind Providence has blessed our
people with abundant crops; the generons soil has poured ils fr11its and grain, its
grasses and cotton, into the garners of a happy people, until we may truly say "the
land langhs with fatness." Hence, qniet and contentment reign all over the State.
The toiling farmer, the patient mecfianic, the restle88 merchant, after the labors of
the day, rest secure of a bright fntnre.
The Grand Master bad issued dispensations for seventeen new J,odges, which
shows that Masonry shares in the returning prosperity of the State. Quite· a nnmber
of his decisions upon points of Masonic law are given in the address. We only note
the two following:Qv.estwn: A candidate was rejected by a Lodge In one county, and !emoved to a
new county, and after residing there a year, petitioned a Lodge there. On application to the former Lodge for permission to initiate him, the former Lodge spread the
·ballot, and the petition was rejected by one black-ball. What should the latter
Lodge do? Answer: The second Lodge, within whose jurisdiction the candidate
resided, had absolute jnr!sdiction over the candidate, and could elect or r eject, as they

1876.J

Grand Lodge of California.

saw proper, but should not elect a candidate known to be objectionable to a number of the brethren. The former had no right to spread the ballot in this case.
This decision was reversed by the Grand Lodge, which held, unlike ours," that
a rejected candidate cannot be accepted by any other Lodge without the consent of
the Lodge which rejected him, and that that consent may be either by ballot or show
of hands, at its discretion."
Qv.estio" : Is It a Masonic offense for a brother to as~ist in stealing a Master

.dn81oer: It is ; or to a88ist in stealing anything else from a brother.

And of the Grand Secretary, this :It is greatly to be feared that the deep interest which R.·. W.·. Bro. HARRIS took

the work which had then been determined upon , until the fatal illneBB overtook him

Bro. HARRIS was devoted to the interests of Grand Lodge, and there can be no
manner of doubt that he wore himself ont In its service. He was initiated into

part in _and was a warm supporter of the cause of Masonry. No man labored more
a.bnndantly to advance its interests.
He was mainly Instrumental in establishing this Grand Lodge, and it was his

death , which occurred on Tuesde.y, the eiii:hteenth day of Aagust laat, at hjs residence in Hamilton. He died peacefully, after a brief Illness, borne alike with fortitnde and resignation.

We have before ns the proceedings of the Masonic Convention, and also of the
first Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Dakota. The Convention to organize the Grand Lodge was held at Elk Point on the twenty-second day of Jone, 1876,
six Lodges being represented. Bro. FRANKLIN J . DEWITT, of Yankton, was appointed
President, and Bro. MARK: W. BAILEY, of Canton, Secretary. The Convention nnanimously resolved that ft was "expedient for the good of Masonry that a Grand Lodge
be orpn!zed In Dakota." A Constitution and By-Lawe were then adopted. A section
of tlie latter strikes ue as rather queer. It reads tbns: "No brother of tbie Grand
Lodge shall be elected Grand Treasnrer of the same two years in succeBBion." ·Are
our brethren afraid that the. morals of a brother would be corrupted by a two or
m01·e yeara' lel\se of euch 110 office ! We think if Bro. LAIDLEY should move to that
jurisdiction, that by-Jaw would be repeale.d forthwith. We re-elect him nnanimonely
each year, and inteud to keep on doing so nntil be backs down himself. When our·
Grand Lodge gete hold of a good thing or good man, It bellev.ea in using it or him
indefinitely. We recommend the same courae to our jnvenile brethren In Dakota,·
even eo far 11e a Grand Treasurer ie concerned. Another section may be based on an
old "landmark," bnt Is the sheerest "old fogyism" notwithstanding: "The Master
most have servea as Warden before his election." We prefer to select a good
brother from the floor of the Lodge, rather than an incompetent Warden.
The M.·. W.-. TnoHAB HENDERSON BROWN was elected Grand Master;and the·.R.-.
MA.BK W. BAILEY, Grand Secretary. These brethren and the other Grand
officers, elect and appointed, were publicly installed at the Baptist Churr.h, by Paet

out on its work of Masonic charity and good deeds, and may it increase an hundred

The sixty-ninth Annnal Communication of the Grand Lodge of Delaware was held

The Address of the Grand Master is of fair length and is well written. Much of
it ie taken np with the consideration of the difficulties between Hope Lodge, No. 4,
and a Bro. H. C. FRIES. Complicated and inexplicable accounts seemed to be the

one new Lodge.
On the subject of Intemperance -the cause of the fall of so ml\ny who were once
good Masons and shining lights-the Grand Master expresses these views, which
were heartily endorsed by the Grand Lodge :1 have had my attention called to the fearful strides intemperance is making upon
members of the Craft in this jurisdiction, and have been asked, time 11ud again, to
call your attention to the fact. Brethren, my reply has always been, Masoo.ry is not
a temperance society, tboagh temperance ie one of our cardio"l virtues. Temper·
ance lectures will do the drunkard no good; he most be bronght to his senses by
something more powerful than a mere lecture. He must be taught that if he claims
the right to go to rain himself, he shall not drag his Lodge down with him, and cast
reflection on the whole fabric of Freemasonry. You will ask, how shall we prevent
thie? I answer that the remedy lies with yourselves, In making the selection of
officers tor your Lodges, select the best men yon have, and be p~rtioularly careful in
your selection of .Junior Warden, whose duty it is to euperiotend the Craft whilst at
refreshment; ft Is he who bas charge of the Craft from the moment the Lodge is
closed until ft is opened again. The duties of the Junior Warden are snch that it

We think the following will apply to California as well as to the District of Columbia. The " Masonic beggars " may be of a different class, bot nearly every Lodge

The following report submitted by Bro. ROBBINS, from the Committee on Correspondence, was adopted by the Grand Lodge :Yonr Committee on Masonic Corresponden~e, to whom was referred, at the last
Annual Commnnication, a communication from the District Grand Lodge of New
South Wales (English Constitution), covering a circular letter issued by the District
Grand !\laster, warning Lodges and brethren against the so-called Lodges In that
Colony working under the auspices of the" Lodge of Memphis," the" Grand Lodge
of New South Wales," and the "Grand Lodge of Australia,'' have had the same
under consideration.
H is the settled practice, in the Dependencies of the British Crown, for the Grand
Lodges of England, Ireland, and Scotland, to exercise concurrent jurisdiction, which
is held by them to be 6Zf'lusine as against the rest of the world. This claim the
Grand Lodge of Illinois, in common with all other Grand Lodges, has respected as
valid until the formation of independent Grand Lodges within such Dependencies;
and its declared position on the question of Grand Lodge jurisdiction binds it to the
same policy in thP. future.
Yonr committee have been unable to find any evidence of the formation of an
independent Grand Lodge in New South Wales, by which, and by which alone, the
concurrently exclusive jurisdiction heretofore exercised in that Colony or Province
by the British Masonic powers, could be legitimately impaired.
•
We therefore recommend that the Lodges and brethren of this jurisdiction be
warned that the holding of Masonic intercourse with pretended Masons, made such
in the Lodges complained of in the circular of the District Grand Lodge of New

That old-time style of having squares and parallelograms, instead of the word

The Grand Master had issued dispensations for the formation of nine new Lodges
daring the ye3r, and had refused several other applications therefor. Be had
hauled several Lodges over the coals for the very unmasonic conduct of discussing
the merits of candidates wba had been black-balled, and endeavoring to .discover
the blackballing brother. It had been a custom In many of the Lodges to permit a
suspended Mason to visit the Lodge for years, " provided he did not sit in Lodge for·
three consecutive meetings." These wise brethren were somewhat forcibly reminded
of the troth that a "suspended Mason" was deprived, dnrlng such snspension, of
"all the rights and Privileges of Masonry," and had therefore no right whatever to
be in a Lodge while thus incapacitated.
One question decided, by the Grand Master wonld be, we think, a no~el one in
this jurisdiction. According to the Kentucky law no other oonclnsion could be
reached; bnt as to the "ancient landmarks," we pass the qne!ition over to Bro.
TAYLOR, of Nevada. A worthy, well-qualified Mason, only held the position of
"honorary member" In his Lodge'. He was elected Worshipful Master thereof,
The Grand Master decided that the election was illegal, he being not a " member of
the Lodge" In the only sense recognized by the Constitution. The Grand Lodge
affirmed the decision, bat passed a resolntion substantially regretting that such was
the law in this partlcnlar case. Why not at once declare that the Constitution shall,
whenever convenient, be interpreted in a Pickwickian sense I It would save a world
of trouble.
The "Masonio Widows' and Orphans' Home Infirmary" at Louisville, which had
been damaged by a tornado to the amount of S25,000, was warmly commended to
!he attention of the Grand Lodge. In reference thereto, the Grand Lodge authorIZed the Board of Directors to issue sev~n per cent. bondl!I to the amount of 9100,000,
the Grand Lodge to indorse the same and assume the payment of principal and

member of the subordinate Lodges. The purpOSfl was indeed a noble one ; but we
cannot but think the policy adopted Ila questionable one. We hope, however, that
our open-hearted brethren will have no future canse to regret their action.
We observe by the Grand Treasurer's accounts that representatives are paid a

They have a "Grand Attorney" In this jurisdiction, who reported his action in

The Grand Lodge adopts ~he policy of letting oat Its printing to the lowest bidder. The result is a poorer specimen of paper and printing than comes to us from any

The Committee on Grieyances submitted condensed reports npon thirteen cases

It may not be worth while to discnss at any great length the lnjnry done to the
thrones of Europe and .Asia by the Declaratfon of Independence ; or, whether they
are more firmly fixed and greater in magnitude now than when our lodej>endence
was established ; but, it is seriously to be apprehended that if the Grand ·Lodge of
Ohio takes this, to say the least of it, imprudent step, it will make the . Masonic institutions of this conntry totter far worse than the Declaration of Independence did
the thrones of monarchs, and that no one now living will ever see the injury repaired.
The colored Lodges of Ohio are clandestine, and enongh has been written npon
that;mbject, and sufficient facts elicited from the records of the Grand Lodges of
:Massachusetts and England, to place that question beyond the possibility of a donbt
fn the mind of any intelligent and impartial man; and since they are clandestine, I
cannot see why they shonld be admitted, because they are colored, or becanse they
are numerous and have assumed the title of Grand. We do not, as .Masons, interfere
with the lives, or liberties, or happiness of any one, nor is it either onr duty or our
privilege to legislate for any special class-sectarian, national, political, or shade of
color; and as there is nothing in the Masonic code of any Orand Lodge that debars
a colored man from admission to our mysteries, I cannot bot look npon it as being
wrong for any Grand Lodge to legislate whole bodies Into onr Fraternity, c;r even an
indivliiual, until he has first been admitted at tile working door of a regularly constltn ted Lodge.
The committee that reported favorably In the Grand Lodge of Ohio, state that
"they have the most satisfactory and conclusive evidence that these colored Freemasons practice· t'be very same rites and ceremonies, and have snbstaot!ally the
same esoteric or secret modes of recognition, as are practiced by ourselves and by
the nniverslll family of Freemasons thronp;hont the world." This is, at the eame
time, a strange and bold a.~sertlon, and withont enterinit Into any inquiry as to how
that satisfactory and conclusive evidence was obtained, whether by actual obeerva·
tfon or correspondence, I am at a loBB to conceive by what means or In what manner
they determine to demonstrate Its truth to any oorrect thinking and acting Mason,
beyond "their oum aasert.ion." I know not what influences may be at work In
Ohio, bnt I have very creditable Information that high State office, even the hlghe st,
has been proposed to prominent Maeons In t!ils jurisdiction by iulluential colored
men, claiming to be Masons, as e. reward for a similar recognition her-:.i bot. as yet,
there has not been found any one reckless enough to hazard his own .111.asonic reptttation or Imperil the welfare of the Fraternity, by making snob a proposition before
this Grand Lod~e.
When tho Grand Orient of France first trespa!!i!ed npon this joriedictlon, some
eight years since, and in which the Grand Orient still persists, the qoestloo of color
never entered for one moment Into the consideration of tbe subject on our part.
The offense of the Grand Orient was two·fold : it had Invaded a l!i11ter grand jnris·
diction, and had recognizoed clandestine Masons in doing so.
This will be the fll'llt time that ever the subject of color or negro has been discussed, either by any Grand Mas~r in his address or by the Grand Lodge, and I
most sincerely regret the circumstances that render such a step neceseary; but If
the snppoaed prejudice against onr colored citizens Is to be made the gro11nd work
or excnse for trampling npon the fundamental laws, usages and customs of onr Fraternity I think it is time the Grand Lodge of Louisiana, which is most deeply inter·
ested In the issue, shonld proclaim lier \ferdlct and try the virtue of remonatrance,
even though she tries it lo vain.
It is only necessary to refer to the history of Prince HaU Lodge of .Massachusetts,
and the records of the Grand Lodge of England, to find the most undeniable proof
that these pseudo Masons have no legitimate standing; and if they are to be admitted
on the gMnnd that "all men are born free and eqnal," why not be entirely consistent and admit all clandest!nes, regardless of color, and even other secret socletlee,
lf they will only change their name and induce a willing committee to proclaim Uat

or concubinage have equal hereditary and legal rights with those born iD wedloek,
and that marriage is a useless ceremony.
Ir philanthropy is the spirit, and tlie only spirit at the bottom of this movement,
thuu the leaders of It, both in France and Ohio, are pnrsning a very unwise course.
lf there Is any prejudice against the colored man, it can be abolished it0oner and
more elfectually by legal and conciliatory than by illegal and coercive measures.
Let the colored man alone, so far as Masonry is concerned, to work out his own
destiny and standing In society, aod the day will no donbt come that In this coll!ltry

merit and in.telligence, aDd by being made a Maaon in a lllgally comtitti.ted consttt~

The Grand Master "tells this little story," which we copy with more plee.snr.e

shows a bright side to our Order which we always welcome :Among the many persons who applied for a.id to the Grand Master, nuder the impression that he has an inexhaustible treasury at his command, was a lady, the
widow of a Master Mason, who was not only in great need of pecnnie.ry assistance, but
whose still greater trouble grew out of her separation from her son, a lad of some
twelve yea.rs old, perhaps, who, in the chances of the times, had been ta.ken from
her and re•ided in a remote district of Louisiana. where he was represented to be
in a pitiable condition. The mother's immediate wants were, in some degree,
relieved on application to the Lodges of the city; bat she was still in migery a.bout
her child. She would have go~e to him could she have obtained the means to make
the Jong and expensive journey. In her great trouble the lady asked the Grand Master if there was nothing he could do to help her; and at le.st, to satisfy her for the
moment and at lee.st give her something to hope for, the Grand Master wrote, from
her lips,' an account of her situation, and, encl<;>sing the lady's address, sent the letter
directed to "The Grand Master of the State of Louisiana, at New Orleans." Many
weeks elapsed, and the calls of the mother to know if there was any news and the
uniform answer that had to be given thiit there was none, became at last painful, and
the Grand Master began to regret, almost, that he had raised hopes that seemed
doomed to disappointment; when, one day the lady appeared, as happy a woman as
the Grand Master had ever seen, in hie office; and her boy was at her side. She
had come to thank the Masons for th11 blessing they had bestowed on her in restoring
him. The rest of the story is soon told. The Grand Master of Louisiana had, after a
good deal of difficulty, found the child, (whose condition was folly as destitute as the
mother had described,) in a remote part of the State; had employed the agency of the
nee.rest Lodge; and in due time the little fellow, ragged and bare, almost, was
sent .to New Orleans. Here the Grand Master clethed him respectably, and farni•hed him with a through ticket to Baltimore and the money for his expenses on the
road· and ia a day or two after his arrival here the Grand Master received a letter
from 'bis M.·. W.·. Brother in Louisiana, speaking in the most gratifying ma.nuer of
the bright intelligence of the waif thus restored to a happy mother. This.ap.ecdote
of Ma•onry would be imperfect were the name of the Grand Master of Lomd1ana not
to be mentioned. It is the M.·. w.·. JOHN G. FLEldlNG.
A" Lodge of Relief," ljllder the control of the Grand Lodge, had been established
in the city of Baltimore.

Most Worshipful (}rand MaRtl!T' :-By your kind indulgence I am here to-day to
perform a most grateful duty. Fifty years a.go it was my privilege and very great
pleasure to be numbered with that countless throng assembled on Bunker Hill t1>
witness the laying of the corner-stone of that noble monument erected to commemorate the brave deeds of that invincible band of heroes and patriots, who, upon that
very hill, fifty lee.rs before, made the first formidable armed resistance to British
oppression, an , by their va)or and indomitable courage, taught an arrogan~ and
insolent foe a lesson more lasti 0g than the granite column which transmits to posterity the remembrance of a day never to be forgotten in the history of our beloved
country, and always certainly to be remembered by all good Masons; for there our
most worthy Grand Master, the illustrious statesman, patriot, and soldier, JOSEPH
WARREN, offered his precious young life as a Re.orifice upon the altar of his country's
liberties. Assembled there upon that occasion were the surviving heroes of our
Revolution, conspicuous among whom stood the dignified form of the Marquis de
LAFAYETTE, the early and devoted friend of W ASHISGTON. At the close of the ceremony, and after the delivery of the magnificent oration by Daniel Webster, the
Masonic portion of the assembly unclothed, preparatory to proceeding to what was
more prop!!T'ly known as Bunkm· Hill, where a mmptnous dianer WR!! partaken of by
several thousand persons. As my position, as one of the marshal• of the day, gave
me the opportunity of being near the person of General LAFAYETTE, I received from
him, in that graceful, bland, and affable manner ~o peculiar to himself, the Masonic
apron he had worn during the ceremonies of the day, and whrnh I have faithfully
preserved as a valuable memento of that great man and the interAsting and important event it serves to call to remembrance. But .. as I shall, in all human probability,
soon reach the end of my mortal journey and be compelled to leave the care of this precious relic in other hands, it has occurred to me that I could.find for it no safer or more
appropriate place of deposit than the archives of the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts;
and I will, therefore, Most Worshipful Grand Master, with yoar permission, commit it
to your custody, that ·it may be placed with your other valuable mementos and
records. I have thought it appropriate, aad that it might be acceptable to the
Grand Lodge,· were I to associate with the apron worn by LAPAYRTT.11 and commit
to the same sacred depository, the toasts, and the remarks connected therewith,
otrnred at the dinner tab1e by the President and orator of the day, DANIEL WEBSTER,
and by General ~AF&YETr£, tlte most distinguished guest of the occasion-each in
the handwriting of their respective authors, which were handed me, as toastmaster, on that occasion, at the time of their delivery, by those distinguished gentlemen.

Our brethren of the Bay State seem to have become disgusted with the farce of

perpetually in session. The plan was laid over for further consideration.

MISSISSIPPI.
Onr brethren of this State held their fifty-eighth Annual Communication in Jackson on the second day of February, 1876-the M.·. W.·. A. H, BARKLEY, Grand
Maeter, presiding, and the R.·. W.·. J. L. POWER being Grand Secretary. Two

The Address of the Grand Master is of more than tho asnal length, but well
written, repaying a careful p erusal. We quote an eloquent paragraph from the
opening of the address, on the true mission of Masonry:Occupying, as Freem11Bonry does, a prominent position among the r ecognized
institutions of the land, and which he.a for its ultimate end the amelioration of the condition and elevation of mankind, it is to be expected that the combined efforts ofthe
Fraternity would be directed to the final accomplishment of this lands,ble undertaking.
Founded on the purest principles of morality, and enforcing its teneta, as Freemasonry does, by precepts based npon and deduced from the divine Jaw, we have sum.cient grounds to foster the hope of great results from the united efforts of ~hose
whose lives "are linked togethor by an Indissoluble chain or sincere affection. "
Viewed simply in the light of a social institution, It has elaims upon society which
call for serious thought and calm investigation. But if we would understand and
appreciate its true mission, our thoughts must take a wider range and grasp those
nobler objects which are t he legitimate offspring of t he great principles on which
the institution reats. The foundation of every virtne is troth. To be good and true
is the first lesson which Masonry teaches. To know and do the troth is the grand
end proposed, and when this shall have been accomplished, then, and noi until then,
will the true mission of the institution of Masonry have been fnlftlled.
These fhougbts, brethren, have been called forth from the fact that the true intent
of the Order is not generally understood ; and in viewing it our minds ·are directed
simply to those features which lie upon the surface, to the otter exclusion of those
nobler ends whiqh are worthy of our most patient study. Should this view of the
subject serve to arrest your attention and bring your minds to a more thorough
investigation thereof, we shall have cause for congratulation that the effort he.a not
b.een altogether in vain.

unnecessary that the waiver be made, therefore, in favor of any specified Lodge.

This was only adding oil to the flames. Again and again did Grand Secretary

that the Grand Lodge had sustained the Grand Master.
Non-intercourse now seemed to be the only alternative, and we began to fear that
we were to have a repetition of the n~pleasant French imbroglio. Bro. GouLEY,
however, having performed his commission and exhausted his Masonic rhetoric,
turned the whole matter over to the Grand Lodge.
We turned at once to the report of its committee, expecting to find it full of
brimstone and wrath, but instead thereof, they " roar yon gently an 'twere a sucking
dove.'' In other words, they and the Grand Lodge of Missouri back down from
their position, and let the Grand Lodge of Scotland go " scot free." We give their
report in full:-

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Missouri:The special committee, appointed to investigate the question of jurisdiction
between the Grand Lodge of Missouri and the Grand Lodge of Scotl11nd, submit the
following report as the result of their deliberation:
.
This question wa8 raised by the Grand Lodge of Missouri in the year 1868, upon
information that a citizen of" Missouri, while on a visit to Scotland, was made a Mason
in a Lodge working under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of Scotland. He
returned to his home, made his Masonic claims knnwn, and our Grand Lodge refused
to recognize him as a Mason. The Grand Lodge of Missouri, believing that its juris·
dictional rights had been infringed by this act of a foreign Grand Lodge, promptly
took the ca•e in hand and ordered a correspondence of enquiry and explanation to
be opened with the Grand Lodge of Scotland. This correspondence and the various
reports upon it have been conductetl by our Secretary and the officers of th11 Grand
Lodge of Scotland with an exemplary exhibition of forbearance and fraternal regard
on both sides. Bnt, after yeara of earnest, patient effort, the question at issue, as it
now stands, is no nearer settled than it was in 1868. We have, however, arrived at
a thorough understanding of all the conditions and interests involved, and may, we
think, proceed safely and honorably to an amicrahle settlement of this long-pending
case. The whole matter rests solely with us, and we owe it to ourselves and Masonry
to treat it in such a manner as shall best promote the harmony and good fellowship
which are distingtrishing characteristics ol' the Masonic Order.
We presented our side of the question with Scotland, as involving a fondly cherished principle of Grand Lodge jurisdiction, for the integrity of which we have had
many serious controversies. Scotland had made a Mason of a citizen of Missouri
who was temporarily sojourning in that country, and,'in view of the principle at stake,
we condemned the act and entered protest against the practice.
Scotland, fully understanding our position on the question of jurisdiction, still
claimed the right to make a Mason of a temporary sojourner, he he a citizen of the
United 8tates or any other country, provided he was found worthy. Citizenship had
nothing whatever to do with the right of any Lodge in Scotland to make Masons

the degrees of Masonry must in all cases be the action of the Lodge after ballot daly
had; and further, that the nata.re oftbe reporte ofinvestigatq,m, whether favorable or
unfavorable, should always be oral; 'neither reduced to wl'lting nor appear on the

We notice that quite a number of Grand Masters and Grand Lodges are taking
simHar ground, viz.: That investigating committee8 should simply state fa,pts, and
make ao recommendation or report, either favorable or unfavorable. We rlo not
concur in this view. We think it is the duty of the committee not only to make
diligent inquiry, but to state their opini3n, orally or in writing, distinctly. The argument that ia case of an adverse report, it would be equivalent to a disclosure of the
ensaing ballot, does not weigh with us. The candidate rejected has no right to kn-0w
who investigated, reported, or voted. And if a lP.aky brother will tell the secrets of
a Lodge, why he would dQ so in any case. We do not believe in legislating on the
idea that all Masons are rascals.

14. Quertion. If the majority of the members of a Lodge are implicated in a

16. If a Grand Lodge restore an expelled brother to the rights aud privileges or

16. A Master of a Lodge, or any member thereof, is liable to Masonic discipline

18. An expelled Mason is masonically dead. When restored, it is to Ma~onic life.

other Lodge, after restoration. To afl!llate, he must make appltoaiioo io the regular
form for that purpose, and may apply in any Lodge.
19. A Mason may be punished for oft'enses committed either against the Craft or
against society, and daring the period of punishment he is deprived of all his Masonic
rights and privileges, bot his obligations, once assumed, cannot be thrown aside. It
is in this way that the expression " once a Mason al ways a Mason " is to be understood. ·

jurisdiction, and a man and Mason well and favorably known to those outside the

the first hour of my manhood to this day, l have spent and been spent in the service

I look back npon that portion of the first, which I fain trust will prepare me for the

cepts of our Divine Religion, her service has best fitted me (if, save by God's mercy
alone, man can be fitted,) to answer with trembling hope to the tremendous declara·
tion: 'Inasmuch as ye have done it onto one of the least of these my brethren, ye
have done it onto me.' "
Written, as that address was, from a bed of protracted and most pa.info! illness,
with a foll consciousness that in all human probability he would never rise from that
bed, these words of oar now dec•ased Past Grand Master fell npon the ears of his
brethren with. monrnf'nl P.rophetic ring, and should be treasured in everv Mason's
heart, as fnll of deep sigmficance and of great cheer.
Very soon the life's work was ended ; the span was passed; and time ended and
eternity began for him on Saturday, 14th li'ebrnary, 1874. On Sonday, 15th February, 1874. his funeral obseqnies were performed in the presence of a great and sorrowing throng of his brethren, and of his follow-citizens and friends. Then, at his
own request, without ostentation or parade, some of his brethren laid him to. his rest,
silently casting into his grave the evergreen symbol of that immortality which he
learned to believe in from the lessons derived in the Lodge.
Bnt it was not ia Masonry alone that he stood prominent. His lotelllgenoe, energy,
and chara.8\er gave him, in the community in which he lived, a more than ordinary
share of the confidence of his fellow-citizens. In whatever was calculated to promote the pnblic weal, he took an active interest, and his hand wearied not in the
effort to foster those things which he believed calculated to advance its prosperity.
To his brethren his Masonic life is foll of deep interest. In the studies and duties
it imposed on him, he had been gradnally led to know tbat the end of life is not
death. Masonry was more dear to him, because it had first induced in him serious
reflections npon the momentous issues of the resurrection. Lacking beyond the
dark portals of the grave, he was brought to seek that truth only to be fonnd in the
Temple not made with hands. The significance of his words of farewell are then to
be treasured in every Mason's heart, as the utterance of an intelligent, candid-minded
JDan, bearing testimony to the services '!hich Masonry had rendered to him. Deeply
impressed with the trnst required of him when he entered a Lod!fe, he grew to
thoroughly understand the symbolism of the lost word, and the f!11th demanded of
him when In darkness as to Masonic light, became to him a lesson to seek a surer
foundation than a substitute. With eyes steadfastly fixed upon the ·greater light, he
bore an exhausting and painful illness with wonderful fortitude and cheerfulness.
While life was full of attractions for him, death had been robbed of its terrors. And
the words which, but a few months prior to his own death, he had nsed when speaking of a deceased brother, were eminently expressive or the aspect with which he
regarded the last enemy: " We make no heathen moan over onr dead; not like the
old Greeks do we bewail .them cut off from ' the beanty of the daylight and the glory
of the sun.' A light shines· in our East. A day star has arisen upon onr gloom.
And in a dim and far-oft' way, thongh It be, we comprehend something of the tremendous troth contained in those words or noble courage, 'to die is gain.'"

We presume our brethren on the Slope are acting with their eyes open. They generally 'know what they are about as well as any Masons in the world. They generally
take care of their steps, and make none that need to be retraced. We still, however,

·California has over and over again placed itself squarely upon the doctrine of
exclnsive jurisdiction, and reiterates it now. Jt must be carried to its legitimate conclnsion. fo harmony with this doctrine, it issues charters to Lodges working in
other languages in its jurisdiction. There is in San Franci•co a French J,odge, a

As might be expected, Bro. CUSHING is "down" on the Ohio propositions. We
give a lJaragraph or two to show how strongly our Southwestern brother fetls, and
yet how well and Masonically he talks:ls this regular or spurlons Masonry 7 We have no means of ascertaining save by
what m•nifests itself on the surface. The Ohio Grand Master and others of that
Grand Lodge Reem to claim that it is regular. The German Grand Lodge jumps at
the conclusion that it is regnlar. Have they tried it? Do they know the terms of
admission? Are they the same as those of all other Masonry derived from the Grand
Lodge of England? Do these colored Grand Lodges admit only men who are free
born, of lawful age and under the rongue of good report? ' If so, they can claim our
attention. If not, they cannot. If so, we cannot question the right of those who
like to recognize them. If not»those who do recognize them place themselves out
of intercourse with us. These- are the points ancf the only points to be disoussed.
If colored Masons can bring np a clean record on these points, we will then inqnire
further into their claims. If they cannot, they can certainly not pince themselves
upon the level or demand lo be received upon the square. Not only must those asking recognition present a clear record as to themselves, but as to their associates as
well. We cannot recognize those who consort with spurious Masonry. Tested by
these p.oints this whBle colored fllbric is.of no real weight. It may be an amusement
to those who partioipate in it. It is not Masonry, and Masons must be careful how
they oonnwnance it, or they may place themselves nnder the ban.
We do not argue the indignity of race. We confess we do not recognize such indignity. A colored man, who is a man, shall have from us all the respect, and no
more, a white man can claim. Because he is colored, he shall not be petted-that
would be to indignify him at once. Because he is colored, he shall have nothing
more, and nothing less, than shall a white man, because he is white: Bot for the
reasons that we wonld not hold Intercourse with pretended Masons, who wonld initiate the maimed, the halt, the blind, or women, so we will not hold intercourse with
pretended Masons, who initiate those born in slavery and inheriting ages of mor11l
and mental inferiority. It is the misfortune of many good men to be of such physical
defects as to nnfit them for membership. Grant that it is the misfortune of half of
these 13,000 colored so-called Masons, and possibly nine-tenths of them, to have been
born in slavery, That is that with which we have nothing to do. We belong to a
society instituted of those not snbject to such misfortunes. We owe them nothing.
They have no more right with, of, or about us than any other profane.

Jurisprudence:Power, however acquired, ever tends to centralization, and we think the Fraternity

Master is any more the Grand Lodge ad interim, by inherent rig)lt, than the Worshipful Master is bis Lodge by the same right, when his Lodge is not in seseion.

they are only conferred by the le.ndm&:rlte and usage, &IIdare not possessed by e.ny inherent right, either ez-ojficio or otherwise.
From these and other considerations we must deny that the leflielative powers of
any Grand Lodge "extend to every case of legislation not expressly delegated by
itself" to its constituent Lodges. We would say, rather, that a.II powers properly
exercised by a Grand Lodge are only such as are delegated by her constituent Lodges
and by usage; and all powers not thus expressly or impliedly granted, rem~ in tile
Craft in the subordinate Lodges where they origj.nate.

In most Lodges the W. M. takes the Ee.et at the appointed hour, calls hie Lodge t.o

character, the very mainspring of the institution, is ignored.

to those who are already Me.eons.

throw open the doors of our Lodge rooms and have our wives, daught.ere, sisters,
and mothers meet us in a social way. See to it that your officers are men of exemplary character, intelligent, and respected in the community. Avoid all quarrels and
!llseeneions; make the Lodge meetings interesting to. the Fraternity; reoeive none
mto the Order but those who are worthy and well qualified.
