•
tion and work of the Germau Diet. The conclusion being the pith of the whole, :ie
as follows ::Eight bodies claiming to be Masonic Grand Lodge• in Europe have formed a
Masonic Diet, or grand governing national Masonic authority, which assumes powers
over, and regulates the right• and privileges of, the inferior bodies that have surrendered these rights to this Diet. Among the extraordinary powers claimed by
this German Masonic Diet, or League, is "the right of jurisdiction," or a control
over it. This Diet has the disposition, it would seem, to go into any Grand Lodge
juri<diction of the States of the United States and set up Lodges, under the i;>lea of
nationality, that Masons so organized into a Lodge are Germans, or work m the
German tongue, and therefore owe allegiance to this German Grand Diet. Thie
api:>ears to be the logical deduction from the claim of the "right of jurisdiction."
It is also claimed by this Diet that •'the object and aim of this League is to
secure and promote the unity and Masonic joint action of the Lodges in Germany,
and to assume in common a Masonic attitude toward the Grand Lodges outside of
Germany;" that" it is (;lxclusively the business of the German Grand Lodge League
to determine whether new alliances shall be formed with Grand Lodges outside of
Germany, and whether those already formed are, to be dissolv~d." The Grand
Lodge Diet is the organ of the Grand Lodge League, and this Grand Lodge Diet
consists of the eight Grand Masters and the two Master Masons, elected by each
Grand Lodge.
The Grand·Lodges which ai·e assumed once to have been supreme and sovereign
bodies, but which have now surrendered some of their inherent powers which are
inseparable from Masonic sovereignty, are:1. • The Grand National Mother Lodge of the Prussian States, zu den di·ei
WeUkugeln, at Berlin.
2. ·The Grand Lodge of Saxony, at Dresden.
S. The Grand Lodge of Hamburg, at Hamburg.
4. The Grand Lodge of the Eclectic U.nion, at Frankfort-on-the-Main.
6. The Grand Lodge of Freemasons of Germany, at Berlin.
6, The Grand Lodge of Freemasons zur sonne,at Bayreuth.
7. The Grand Lodge of Prussia, called Royal Yurk zur Freu11dschaft, at

Berlin.

8. The Grand Lodge zur Ji)i.ntracht, at Darmstadt.
Whatever may be the future relations of this Diet with lawfully organized Grand
Lodges, it is very evident to every member of our G.rand Lodge, that there can be
no longer any Masonic intercourse with, or ;recognition by, the R. W. Grand Lodge
of Free and Accepted Masons of Pennsylvania, and the Masonic jurisdiction thereunto belonging, of either this Diet or the emasculated Masonic Bodies that are its
present constituents, during the existence of this Diet with its present character.
The Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania is old enough, and wise enough to understand
her O\'nl duty, and no greater benefit can be conferred by her on her eist.er Grand '
Lodges, both in the States of our Union and wherever Masonry is to be maintained
on the landmarks, than by declaring in her conservative action that no recognition
can be given to thiR Diet or its constituents. All .time has proven that the abandonment of Masonic law brings its own condemnation.
This report was adopted by the Grand Lodge, and of "Course, entire non-intercourse declared as to all Masons hailing from the above named Grand Lodges.

Bro. WILuAM A. DAVIES, from the special committee to whom had
been referred the Address of the Grand Master, presented the following report:To the M. ·• W. •. (}rand Lodge of Oalifornia:Yoor committee, appointed to review and apportion the annual message of the
Grand Master, and to recommend it~ reference, respectfully report that they have
given th.at excellent paper all tlie attention permitted by the limited time at their disposal. They most heartily echo his sentiments of praise and rejoicing at the wonderful progress of our coontry thns far npon the highway of snccessflll political
experiment-the result of the labors of brave, thoughtful, earnest, and honest menand they iook forward with all his hope to its foture crowning glories.
In this centennial year, we of the Grand :{..odge of California, in the full enjoyment
of ail the civil and religious freedom consistent with the restrainh of law, may well
give heed to the words of praise with which our Grand :Ma ;t~r prefaces his message,
and, with him, devoutly recognize the protecting care of our great Ruler as we silently
respond-God save the nation.
In his remarks of a general nature your committee are reminded that, dnring his
t erm of office, our organization has been under the supilrvisi.on of a zealous, watchful,
and able executive-one who has not only noted its progress, hot has carefully ob~erved the restraint3 upon its growth by the evils incident to all associations. They
commend a carefal study of this message to all the brethren of this jurisdiction, and
they especially desire to invite the attention of the members of the Grand Lodge to the
reasoning ofthe <:rand Master npoa a few of his most imporhnt suggestions.
First.-Your committee commend the propo•ition to· abolish the affiliation fee,
thereby aiding, in some measure, to correct the great' evils of non-affiliation.
Becond.-They agree with bis views in regard to the amount of Lodge dues. A
sound and healthy Masonic Lodge mnst have a treasury sapp\ied from an absolute
revenue, such as regnlar does saftlcient to secure it from peouniary embarasement,
without reliance npon tile sale of degrees.

ffiird.-They coincide with the Grand :Master as to the gEneral effectiveness and
universality of our ritual. He has had ample opportunity to witness such of its imperfe ctions as may exist, and he arrives at the conclusion that any change, if made,
should be of the slightest; and they would simply add to the Grand Master's suggestion. that it would perha!Js be better still to let it alone than to open a door to
encourage the bottled ap wisdom of the work·makers, since we have gotten al~ng so
well dnring the last ten or twelve years •

. That so much as relates to dispensations for new Lodges, be referred to the Committee on Charters.

Bro. WILLIAM ·A. DA.vms, from the Committee on Jurisprudence,
presented the following report :. To the M. ·• W. •• Grand Lodge of California :The Committee on Jurisprudence have given carefnl consideration to sundry
matters referred to them, and respectfully report thereon as follows:I. As to an amendment to the Constitution p~oposed by Bro. RoLLm DUNSBBB at
the last Annual Communication. See proceedings of 1875, page 102•
This amendment proposes to so change the organic law of this jurisdiction, in
respect to ballots upon petitions for membership, as to declare the petitioner elected
unless there shall be at least three black balls in the ballot box, and to give to the .

492

Proceedings of the ·

[Oot. 11,

petitioner the right, when there a~e but three black balls in the box, to demand of
the pal'ties who c88t them their reasons for so doing.
This proposition, if adopted, would \fOrk a very radical change in our.proceedings.
Our Constitution now requires that the ballot shall be unanimous. If but one black
ball appear in the box, the Master must, before declaring the result, order a reballot
to determine if perchance the black ball were cast by mistake; but he can permit no
discu88ion of the matter in his Lodge, nor can he delay the rl\ballot to another meeting. (Const. Sec. 3, A.rt· III, Part III.) The ballot mu~t be secret, and, when the
result has been declared, no member of the Lodge can divulge his vote or the reasons
for it. He cannot be asked or allowed to give his reasons. (Const. Sec. 2, Art. IL
Part V.) ·
These reqnireme11ts seem to your committee to be just what the exigencies of the
case demand. From time immemorial they have been a part of the fundamental law
of Masonry in all the world, and ii would not he wise now to adopt new rules in their
shad. ·A M88onic Lodge is a family, and no one should be admitted as one of its
componentl without the consent of all its members. Discord and confusion would
be sure to follow if the rule proposed by the amendment were to become the law;
and your committee recommend that the proposed amendment be not adopted.
I. Concerning certain communications from the Grand Lodge of Manitoba relative to recognition by this Grand Lodge.
At the last Annual Communication this commiltee examined the documents
placed in their hauds relative to the formation and esbblishment of this new Grand
Lodge, and reported that the proceedings were regular and that the best interests
of Masonry seemed to require the establishment of a Grand Lodge in that Province
of the Dominion of Canada; but, as all the constituent Lodges held charters from the
Grand Lodge of Canada, it was thought advisable to wait until recognition should be
extended by that mother Grand Lodge.
Now a communication from the Grand Secretary, Bro. JOHN H. BELL, addressed
to onr Grand Secretary, advises ns that such recognition was extended by the Grand
Lodge of Canada at it~ Communication in Jnly, 1875, and we find it so recorded by
• referring to the proceedings of that Grand Lodge. Bro. BELL thinks it strange that
such action on the part of the Grand Lodge of Canada had escaped our attention, and
we can only excuse ourselves by str.tlng the fact that the proceedings of that Grand
Lodge had not, at the date of our report, been received by our Grand Secretary.
The Grand Lodge of California was then, 88 ever, disposed to respect the rights of its
sister Grand Lodges, and it recognized the right of the Grand Lodge of Canada to
control the action of its own subordinates. Your committee are glad now to learn
thatthe Grand Lodge of Manitoba has been rceognized by the.mother Grand Lodge;
and the only objection to recognition being thus removed, they propose and recom·
mend the adoption of the followiO:g resolution:Resollled, That the Grand Lodge of California h88, with great pleasure, recognlzect
the Grand Lodge of Manitoba as a just and legally constituted Grand Lodge, nnd gives
it hearty welcome to the family of Grand Lodges; and that the Grand Master be
reqn·e sted to appoint some brother resident within the Province of Manitoba as our
llepresentative near that Grand Lodge.

IV. Relative to certain communications lately received from the Grand Orient of
Egypt.
Two communications from this Grand Orient have been placed in our hands;
olie i'equestiug au interchange of representatives, and the other announcing the
recognition of that Grand Orient by the Grand Lodge of England.
The system of foreign representatives is of recent origin, but seems to have met
with very general favbr. As the dnties of such representatives are generally under·
stood and performed, the office Is one of honor simply. It ought to be something
more. It ooght to be useful to the power appointing as well as honorable to the per·
son appointed, and the rights and duties of persons holding such appointments ought
to be more fully determined. Your committee recommend that the Grand Master be
reqnested to appoint some proper person to represent this Grand Lodge near the
Gr11nd Orient of Egypt.
V. Ooncerning snndry matters relating to the Grand Orient of the Argentine
Republic.
Several commnnications and documents relating to the alfairs of this Grand Orient
have been placed in our hands. These show that the Masons of that Republic are
not at peace among t}\emselves, but we have been unable to gairt from these com·
munications and documents, or from any other source, sufficient information to enable
ns to form an intelligent jndgmeut .in regard to the difficulties existiag there, or to
determine whether they are of such a character as to call for any action on the part
of this Grand Lodge. Your committee therefore recommend that these papers, with
such others as may hereafter be received from the same source, be referred to the
Committee on J arisprudeuce for the coming year.
VI. Relative to certain troubles within the jurisdiction of the Grand Orient of
Spain.
A circular-letter from the Grand Master of this Grand Orient informs us that a few
turbulent brethren have raised the standard of"revolt against the authority of that
body. Tho difficnlty' is one of purely local concern. This Grand Lodge coold not, if
it wonld, render any assistance in suppressing it, and no action In regard to it seems
to be necessary.
VIL Relative to the consolidation.of Tuolumrre Lodge, No. 8, and Mount JeJfBr·
..son Lodge No, 107.
Yoor committee have examined the reported proceedings of the8e Lodges, looking
to consolidation, and find that both have pursued substantially the course recom •
mended by this committee in their report on tile consolidation of MaryBVille and
Corinthian Lodges, in 1874. See proceedings of that year, page 661.
Committees of conference were appointed in September, 1876. These committees
agreed upon and reported the terms of consolidation, and their reporh were adopted
in October of that year. An order was made in each Lodge directing the Secretary
to notify all it3 members that the subject would come up for final action at the st1ted
meeting in February. 1876; and we presome that such notice was given, thongJi it is
not so stated in either of the reporh. Prior to the meeting in February, just threefonrths of the members of .MOunt JejferBoi> Lodge, and·very nearly or quite all the
members of Tuolumne Lodge, had signified their assent to the consolidation; and at
the meetings in February the final vote was had in each Lodge in favor of consolidation upon the terms agre11d upon. The terms were that the new Lodge shoold bear
tile name and number, and shonld ret&in the charter and seal, of Tuolumne ~odge,
No. 8, and should hold its meetings in the ball of that Lodge at Sonora, and that all

VIII. Relative to the consolidation of Saint John's Lodge, No. 37, and Si.skiyou
Lodge, No. 105.
At the Annual Communication in 1874,, transcripts of the proceedings of these·
two Lodges for consolidation under the name of St. John'11 Lodge, No. 37, were ex·
amined by this committee, and found so defective that the papers were returned to
the Lodges for further action. The papers were defective because they did not
show that the notice, required by the Constitution, to all the members of the Lodges
had been given-nor that three-fourths of the members of each Lodge had aseented
In writing to th~ proposed consolidation-nor that there had been any final action of
one of the Lodges.
Section 11, Article II., Part Ill., of the Constitution, positively requires that " the
members of each. Lodge shall have at l east three months' notice before the stated
meeting at which such proposition is to be acted upon," and it requires, also, "the
assent in writing of at least three-fourths of all the members of each Lodge_to adopt
such proposal for consolidation."
These are requirements which cannot be dispensed with, and the compliance with
them onght in all cases to appear upon the records of the Lodges and in the tran&cripts of proceedings sent up to the Grand Lodge.
On the fifth ~ay oi' June, 1875, the matter of consolidation was referred by St.
John's Lodge, No. 37, to Bro. Hli:NRY L. TICKNER, its present Master, who, on the
sixteenth day of the same mouth, made to his Lodge a very full and carefully prepared report, which we specially commend as a model report of its kind. From this
we learn that notice waa, in fact, given to the members of each Lodge for the time
required, but was given by the committees, and not by the Secretaries, through
whom such not.ices shonld always be given; that at least three-fourths of the
members of each Lodge signified their assent, in writing, tn the consolidation; prior to
the meetings for final action; and that at such meetings the question of cou~olidation
was in fact acted upon in each Lodge, and that ea.ch voted In favor of it. Your committee, therefore, now recommend that the proceedings of those Lodges relative to
consolidation be approved, and propose the adoption of the following resolutions:Resolved, That the proceedings of SL John's Lodge, No. 37, and Siaklyou Lodge,
No. 105, relative to consolidation, be .and hereby are approved, and that the consolidation of said Lodges take effect on the first Saturday in December, 1876, the day of
the annual election of officers in St. John's Lodge, No. 37.
Be.solTJed, That the Lodge formed by the consolidation of said Lodges take the
name of Saint John'.s Lodge, No. 37, and be allowed to retain the charter and seal of

Your commitree are pleued to note a manifest improvement in the tr11Dscripts of
tria.!-records sent up to the Grand Lodge, as compared with those of former years,
showing that the efforts of our Grand 8ecrete.ry and of the chairmen of this committee have been of great benefit. Most of the errors which appear have been
merely clerical, and in all co.sea, where the attention of the proper officers has been
called.to them, the evidence necessary to correct them has been promptly furnished.
Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal of Bro. A.BRA.RAM: D. Fox from
the action of the acting Mll8ter of Valley Lodge, No. 135, in dismissing the commissioners and failing to proceed with the charge preferred against Bro. NATlliNIEL
BIOOON HARBOLD, December 7th, 1875, upon full consideration of the same report
as follows :.
·
The record is imperfect, the charge is not sent up, and there is no proof of any
order to issue and serve the suJDmons with copy of charge. But, as nothing in the
appeal ta.!ren turns upon the nature or snfficiency of the charge, and 118 the accused
appeared at the tima fixed for tria.!, we deem it proper to determine the case simply
npon its merits.
At the opening of the trial the Senior Warden of the Lodge presided, in _the absence of the Master. He had also presided at the meeting of the Lodge for the election
of commissioners. Upon his request, and aga.lnst the objection of the accusedi all
persons were obligl:d to re*e from the Lodge-room except the commissioners, the
Bocrete.ry, and the accused. The accused, as the record shows, offered as a bar to the
proceedings the averments that the com.mission had been illega.!ly elected, he not
having been especia.!ly notified that the specia.! meeting called for the election of com·
missioners was for the purpose of trying him for unmasonic conduct, and that he
had not been legally notified of the trial, the summons not having been personally
served on him. "O"pon this, the acting Master ruled the bar to the proceedings 1111
valid, and dismissed the comml>sion; and this constitutes the record.
The action as above stated is erroneous in every respect. The accuser had the.
right to be present at the trial and to a hearing np to its conclusion. The accused
had no absolute right to be informed 118 to whom a charge had been preferred
against, when the special meeting of the Lodge was called for the purpose of electing
commissioners to try a brother ror unmasonic conduct. The summons was served
by mail and was effectual, 118 is shown by the fact that the party appeared and
acknowledged the receipt of the summons, and objected only to thi; mode of its
service. The object of the summons wll8 accomplished and no injustice or harm
was done to the accused; and the commissioners -s hould, therefore, have proceeded
with the trial.
.
'
.As the same commission cannot probably be convened to try the case, your
committee deem it advisable'that a new commission be constituted and that the case

1867.]

Grand Lodge of Oaliforni,a.

499

proceed. The action complained of was erroneous and sho~ld be set aside, and your
oommittfe therefore recommend the adoption of the fol!owmg resolution:Resolved; That the action of the acting M118ter of Valley Lodge, No. 135, in dismissing the commission elected to try a certain charge preferred against Bro. N ATHiliIEL SIGGON HARROLD, be and is hereby disapproved, and that the sa.ld Lodge is directed to proceed to a proper .trial of the accused on the charge pr!lferred against him.

Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal of Bro. DAVID H. SHAW from the
action of Evening Star Lodge, No. 186, in acqoitting Bro. Jums ALDEN DIGGLEB
from a charge of nnmasonic conduct preferred against him, report 118 follows:The gravamen of the charge consists in the use of severe language respecting a
tran~action arising out of the alleged encloeing and claiming of a public street, or
what W118 claimed to be one. The language used on both sides was unjusti.fiable and
improper; yet that the word "stolen"-nsed in that connection by the accusedwas to some extent qualified by the explanation that he considered that, as long as be
(the accuser) kept that piece of ground nuder fence, he was stealing it from the pub1\c, was evidently regarded by the commission 118 not importing a crime, but rather as
an unjustifiable claim to property about which there might be honest difference of
opinion.
Your committee regret that such opinions were not more guardedly expressed on
both sides, and they trust that the brethren will see the propriety of mutual reparation
and apology. In the present aspect of the case they can only affirm the judgment of
the commission and recommend the adoption of t he following resolution;Resolved, That the action of Eoening Star Lodge, No. 186, in acquitting Bro.
JAMES ALDEN DrooLES from the charge preferred against him therein be affirmed,

Your committee, to whom was rererred the protest of Bro. DAvm K:ETrr.EliuN againsi
the action of Woodbridge Lodge, No. 131, in ordering a warrant drawn upon ihe
Lodge fnnds for payment for a supper npon the ocC1111ion of the installation of its
officers, have only to report that the law on this subject is very plain, and ihat ii
seems singular that such a case should arise. At the cost of encumbering our
proceedings, but with the hope of preventing any recurrence of ibis error, your
committee refer to the proceedings of 1873, report of the Committee on Jurispru"
dence, pages 17~, as follows :"A Mll8onic Lodge is established for certain purposes o! charity and society, and
~there its funds for the promotion of those purpoi!es. For such purposes it has t?e
malienable right to expend all its available funas, and, if need be, to call upon it.a
members for nnusua.! contributions. It holds its funds in trnst for those purposes
and none olhel' ; and whenever it uses them or allows them to be used for any other,
It becomes false to its trust and should be held "to strict account. It is humiliating
wknow, and knowing to confess, that there could be found a majority in any Lodge

500

P~oce<:dings of the

[Oct. 12,

in_this State, with so little apprecia,tion of the spirit an~ objects of ~asonry, and

with ·so little regard for the welfare and good name of ·thell' -Lodge. as to consent to
divert its funds from their legitimate uses and employ them for their private amusements and gratifications. It is well enough, if the members of a'. Lodge choose to
give dinners or collations to their newly imtalled officers and can afford to pay for
them, that they should do so; but it is simply shameful for them to take the funds
of the Lodge to pay the bills." ·
It seems strange that, even without such an explicit declaration of the law on this
subject, cause for such a protest should have arisen, but, as it is before your committee, they have only to report that the action of the Lodge in this ma,tter was improper
and reprehensible. They refrain from recommending any action upon the subject
at this time, trusting that tho brethren of Woortbridge Lodge will see their way clear
to reimburse the Lodge funds for what bas thus been abstracted, and hoping that
there will be no recurrence of a complaint of this nature.

SECTION 2. Tho table of fees for non-members shall be as follows: For the
degree of Fellow Craft, twenty-five dollars ; for the degree of Master Mason, twentyfive dollars; and for affiliation by dimit, one dollar.
Who the "non-members" are to whom fees are to be charged, and what the

exactly understand; but they recommend that said Section 2 be stricken out, and
that the words " for affiliation, one dollar," be added to Section 1.
Your committee also find that the various amendments proposed by sundry
Lodges to their by-laws, as set forth in the Address of the Grand Mast.er and the
Report of the Grand Secretary, which were referred to them, are in conformity with
the Constitution of the Grand Lodge; and they recommend that they be all approved,
with the single exception of an emendmen t to the by-laws of EJperanza ltaliana, No.
219, which imposes a fine (in the guise of dues) upon the officers of that Lodge for
non-attendance at Lodge meetings, sickness or absence from the city alone excusing
them. Your committee are unanimously of the opinion that this amendment should
not be approved by the Grand Lodge, as it is believed that, should it be adopted, it
would establish a precedent that would not be subservient W the best interests of
Freemasonry;

to this committee with the usual instruction t.o consider and report thereon for the
final action of the Grand Lodge :A brother, who is represented as having boon an honest, correct, and hard-working man, regardful of his duties to his family, was suspended by his Lodge for non·
paymeot of dues, and subl!equently removed to -the jurisdiction of another Lodge.
While thus under suspension he was accidentally injured, and immediately thereafter
money was sent by a brother to the Lodge of which he had been a member, to pay
the delinquent dues, which money was received and receipted for by the Seoretary.
Three hours after the departure o~ the messenger with th.e money, and before it had

1876.J

Grand Lodge of Oaliforni.a.

511

been paid, the injured brother died, which fact being made known t.o the Secretary,
he, by direction of the Mast.er of the Lodge, returned the money and refused to
record the restoration. The matter having been submitted"to the Grand Master for
his decision, it was his opinion· that, the dues having_been paid and reoeipted for
after death, the disability was not removed; that death . precluded a. reinstat.ement;
and tha.t the first action of the Secretary, in reoeiving and receipting for the money,
having been performed under the impression that the brother was alive, in a strictly
legal sense was null and void. He decided, as is evident, against his own sympivthies, but strictly according to the, letter of our Jaws, and thorefore sustained the
action of the Master, who had declined t.o consider the acts performed sufficient to
complete the restoration of the suspended brother.
In the opinion of your committee, if this was a case in which a brother who waa '
oapable of making his defense wa8 put on trial for charges involving a breach of the
moral law of our fraternity, there would be no alternative other than to consider the
case under the a.pplioation of strict and literal rules. The Grand Lodge has repeatedly said that the fundamental laws of Masonry, respecting its morality, should be
construed strictly, but always with charity; and, in respect t.o its government, with
liberality and in the true spirit of the enactments and customs. Your committee
think tha.t the case which they have now to consider involves no poiiit of morality.
That the tardiness or remissness of the unfortunate brother will count against him at
the great day none will suspect; but that it may, in some measure, operate prejudic·
ially to the interests of his widow and orphans is possible.
,
·
The langu&gtl of the Constitution is that "any Mason thus suspended, who shall
at any time pay the arrearages,due at the time of his ouspeosion, t.ogether with such
further dues as would, had he r etained his membership, have accrued &!(a.inst him to
the da~ of such payment, or who shall have had such arrearages or dues remitted by his
Lodge, shall by either of these acts be restored." It seems to the committee that the
only question to be considered, and the one which should govern the case under the
els.use quoted, is whether a brother under suspension, who, three hours before
his death, remits to the Secretary of the Lodge the amount of money necessary t.o
entitle him to restoration, complies sufficiently with the true spirit of the enactments
and cust.oms? This is the question which is presented by the record; and. while the
committee have in view the decisioh by the Grand Lodge that a Ma.son dying under
suspension cannot be restore,d by any action subsequent to his death , they believe
that the essential and nec8!1sary requirement by the Oonstitution had in this case been
sufficiently: complied with previous to the death j and they are of the opinion that
restoration should not be denied.
·
Your committee have considered the proposed amendment t.o the fourth subdivision of 8ection 1, Article V, Part IV, of the Constitution, offered by Bro. LEw:ls
F. JOJ11ES, providing that that subdivision shall read as follows:4th. To collect and receive all moneys due to the Lodge and pay them over to
the Treasurer quarterly. .
.
8uch an amendment would have the effect, in the opinion of the committee, of
me.king the Secretary in a measure the custodian of the funds of the Lodge. It is
evidently the intention, as the Constitution now stands, and it was certainly the old
cust.om, that the Secretaries shall pay over the funds which come into their hands as
fast as they are received. The committee see no good reason for any change, and
thus report to the Grand Lodge.

Appertaining to the same subject, there was also referred to your c.ommittee a

Resol:oed. That the dues of Lodges to the Grand Lodge should be payable In such
money aa they receive for dues from members, provided that it be legal money of
the United States.
It requires little consideration on the part of' yoor committee to enable them to
aay that the letter ol the Grand l:!ecretary was, as might have been expected from
him , a very proper and busineBB-like communication, which sets forth well and cone1118ive!y all the argument that there can be upon the subject.
The adoption of the resolution above presented would make it necessary that
the whole financial busine~s of the Grand Lodge should be transacted upon a different basiti than that of other busineBS throughout the State. Lodges would he at liberty to pay their does to the Iirand Lodge in silver, or legal tenders, or national
bank notes, and the result would be to compel an additional Increase of dues to pay
the discount upon such depreciated currency; otherwise the revenue would be im·
paired. The question then at issue is whether it is expedient or advisable to use
a dilferent money in transacting the financial business of the Grand Lodge from that
acknowledged and accepted by the commercial community in which we live. Your
committee are unanimously of the opinion that it is not, and they therefore oft'er the
following resolution and recommend its adoption:ReaolrJed, That the dues to this Gl'and Lodge are payable only in United States
gold coin or its equivalent.

Relief which, by reason of their location in the State, have extraordinary demands ma.de
upon t~em for aid, thereby enabling them to extend the band of charity to all in
distress who are found worthy. They fear that &n indiscriminate appropriation to
every organization ,calling itself a "Board of Relief," situated in difi'erent towns
throughout the State, will cause a renewed complaint that the expenses of the Grand
Lodge are exceBBive, and that it might also deprive many of our brethren of the
opportunity of giving their private alms, as they otherwise would without this aid,
thereby in a measure preventing them from realizing " that it is more blessed to give
than to receive." Believing, however, that when in doubt it is better to err on the
side of charity, and as the funds of the Grand Lodge will justify the appropriation,
they offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption :Resol·veq, That the sum. of three thonsand dollars be appropriated to and divided
among the several Ma.sonic Boards of Relief as follows :To San Francisco, ...•.•.•••••.• $2000 00 To Marysville,.. ................ $ 125 00

Proceedings of the

Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal of Bro. AUGUSTO D. SPLIVALO
from the action of Speranza Italiana Lodge, No. 219, in suspending him from all the
rights and privileges of Masonry, have co~slde~ed the same and report as foll?ws :The appellant is accused, in two specificat1ons, of the wrongf~I app~opr1atlon of
moneys of a certain benevolent society. It appears that the said society expelled
him from its membership for these alleged appropriations, and that the Master of the
Lodge, as one of the trustees of that society, voted for his expulsion. The appellant
objected to the Master presiding over the trial commission of t~e L.odge, on the
ground that he had prejudged the c11se by having so voted. The obJection was overruled and the trial proceeded with.
The Grand Lodge, in the year 1874, clearly declared the principles governing
thili point. The accused has a right, at any time before t~e coi;nmence~ent of the
trial, to object to any commissioner upon the ground that he 1s so biased, ~r mterested,
or prejudiced that it would be unfair for him to act. The same objeotiona may be
made to the Master, and the same reasons which would disqualify a brother fro~
acting as a commissioner disqualifies the Master from presid'.ng at ~he trial. In t~1s
case the Master had prejudged the case, and for this reason 1t was unproper for huu
to preside. The commission, and all trials in Masonry, most be so constituted and
·conducted as to be reasonably free from any saspicion of unfairness, .bias, prejudice,
or partiality.
It also appears that, after the close of the testimony on behalf o! the pros~cu­
tion, 'the accused moved for a continuance of two days to present his defense. It
was then mW.night. The continuance was refused, whereupon the accused protest:ed
against the proceedings and retired. This refusal was an error. Reas~nable con~n­
uauces should always be granted, to afford the accused an opportunity to exerc1Se
bis right of defense. The commission may meet at and continue th~ir sessions during
such reasonable hours as they in their discretion may deem convement; but to com·
pel the accused, against his consent, to undergo a trial after midnight, is an abuse ot
its discretion.
It also appears that a great number of the brethren of the Lodge are members of
the society 11.lleged to have been wronged; and, under all the oircumstan~es, your
committee deem it best to submit the following resolution and recommend its adoption:..
•
.
Resol1Jed, That the action of Spe'l'anza Italiana Lodge, No. 219, 10 suspendm.g
Bro. AUGUSTO D. SPLIVALO from all the rights and privileges of Masonry, be and is
hereby reversed and set aside, and t1;iat the Grand Master be requested to ~eslgnate
some other Lodge in the city of San Francisco for the r~·nial and determmatlon of
the case at iBBue.
All which is reepectfnlly submitted by
WILLUH 8. WELLS,
WILLIAH T. REYNOLDS,
SilWBL G. HILBORN,
· O<m1miJtee.

.ThEl Grand.Master, stating the purpose· of the Special Communication, a,JJ1·essed the assemblage as follows :_BBETHBEN OF THE GRAND• LODGE OF CALil!'ORNIA :-

SPECIAL

The Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Ma.sons ho.s been convened in Special
Communication to pay the la.st sad tribute of respect. to the remains of JA!ICES LAIDLEY, an old; faithful, esteemed, and beloved officer, who for more than fifteen years has
served as its Grand Treasurer. How well and satisfactorily he tilled that P•)Sition is
attested by the unanimity which attended his successive elections to this high office
in our Grand Lodge.
Brother LAIDLEY, since his arrival in this State in the year 1850, has occnpied
offices of trust and hooor pertaining to national, State, and municipal government,
as well as in our Ma.sonic bodies , a.ncl has held membership in the Order of Odd .Fellows and in several other societies for benevolence and the common good. He was
an earnest, liberal supporter of the Church, both in his individual ·and official
capacity, and in him she will have to moum for the loss of one of her most zealous
and consiRtent adherents .
His public and private charities are as honsehold words in the commnnities in
which he lived; and to the poor, the necessitous, and the afflicted, his heartfelt sympathy and prodigal assis tance will be greatly missed, while the remembrance thereof
will be gratefully cherished in the memory of its host of recipients. And in this
connection may it be truly said that " there is one person now the less to carry ont
the will of God in the world;>' For it has been written-

A few weeks since, iu this place, the deceased was pre90nt at the funeral ceremonies of Bro. FREE:MAN , and many of us will recall his appearance on that occasionhis believed necessitated performl;lllce of duty when the shadow of advancing death
was a.lready.rest.ing on his brow. With streaming eyes, heaving breast. and tremulous words, he then gra.specl my hand, and . pointing i-0 the ca:;ket wh:ch contained
the body of his friend, prophetically said: "T!Je next time it will be me, but I am
ready; God's will be done !" And who will forget his following t11at friend to the
grave, where, so enfeebled by disease as to demand suppo1·t, with fa.I ering steps yet
determined will . he advaneed and gave the touching. mournful spect.acle of a dying
brother dropping the sprig of acacia on the coffin of his dear companion-his final
act of respect and frienddbip.
Only a few days before his death I visited Bro. LAIDLEY, who evinced much
plea.sure in our meeting, and we conversed freely. He spoke of his condition with
the calm resignation of a philo;opher. and with an immovable and cluudleu faith
that made him trustful and ready to obey the decree of Providence. And as I go
into the nuknown future I shall ever have in recollection his parting words, twice
i;epeated with solemn impressiveness, "Goel be with you;" which I then received,
and hope alway• to carrv, as the earnest ble~sing ·of a devoted, loyal M88on.
His wa.s a life overflowing with good deeds. His moral strength and religious
steadfastness 1X1ade his oharity broad and self-denying. He loved what was right and
true for its proper value. Hi< temper wae kindly, genial, patriotio in its best sense,
actuated by a magnanimous, humane nature. He had directness of speech , and
could not be false or disingenuous, selfish or ungenerous. He had po•itive points
and the most strongly-marked pecuFarities. Not the "ten-fold adamant" was
firmer than he was at the time of duty or self-assertion, and with him self-assertion
was a declaration of the instincts and impulses of an upright nature. A truer,
kinder heart beats in no living breast than that which now lies before us cold and
pulseleBB.
True, trusty, and tried, he is entitled to an honorable and loving remembrance

Proceeef.ings ,of t~e

[Dec. 17,

among the Freemasons of California, and we, therefore, are here assembled to perform the Masonic offices of sorrow in testimony of our estimation and affection.
To the bereaved family we extend our warmest sympathy. To offer consolation
would be but formal and ineffectual, for their grief is too sacred for consolation, save
that which descends from Heaven. We may, however, say to them that to live well
is truer good fortune than to live long; and "to live nobly and in life to act greatly,"
the ancien~ said, "was to be· like unto the gods, and so men ascended to the stars.''
We may say to them that the eulogy of their husband and father is his life; his
epitaph is the general grief; his monnment, builded by his own hands, is the ettirnal
statue of truth, justice, and charity.
"May God give unto us wisdom to profit by these influences, e.p.d unto him, our
dead brother, greatly beloved, eternal rest."

The Grand Master then informed the Grand Lodge that our deceased brother had some years ago made a written request, which was
repeated but a few days before his death, that his long-time and intimate friend, Bro. CHARLES Lours WIGGIN, the present Deputy Grand
Master, should conduct the Masonic services at his funeral; and that,
in ready acquiescence with t~at request, he would resign the gavel to
that brother.
The Deputy Grand Master then read that portion of the funeral
service usually given in the Hall, when a procession was formed and
the body of Bro. LAIDLEY was conveyed to Trinity Church, of wltich,
during his life, he htid been an active and most useful member, where
the services of the Episcopal Church were giveu.
Thence the body was conveyed to the Masonic Cemetery by the
Grand Lodge and a very large number of his Masonic brethren,
accompanied by his fellow-members of the Independent Ord.er of Odd
. Fellows, of the Saint Andrew's Society, of the Caledonian Club, and
of the Society of Territorial Pioneers, and by a great number of citizens, where, with the solemn and impressi~e ceremonies of our Order,
conducted by the Deputy Grand Master, the body of our brother was
consigned to the tomb.
The Grand Lodge then returned to its Hall, where, upon motion, it
was ordered that a committee of five be appointed to prepare and present at the next Annual Communication, such report as to them shall
seem meet concerning our late Grand Treasurer and beloved brother,
JAMES LAIDLEY.
